Program kvantitativnog popu9atanja ESB-a i HNB In recent months, comments and suggestions on the need to introduce quantitative easing in Croatia have been emerging more and more frequently in the form recently implemented by the European Central Bank, as implemented by the Fed and other central banks before it. Therefore, here I take the opportunity to once again emphasize the essential reasons why this is not applicable in the Croatian case. First, the CNB's monetary policy expansion does not achieve the same instruments as they are used in quantitative easing policies of the largest central banks. Quantitative easing is used by central banks, which primarily run their policies through the interest rate channel, after the standard channels of action have been exhausted, that is, after the reference interest rate has reached zero level. In this context, quantitative easing in Croatia is neither necessary nor applicable, nor desirable. Why? Because the structure of the CNB's balance sheet is very different, the structure of the domestic financial system is also different compared to the financial systems of large developed economies and, finally and most importantly, because the CNB has a different framework for the implementation of monetary policy that primarily relies on the stability of the exchange rate of the domestic currency, which is the fundamental channel for achieving our legal mandate of price stability and overall financial stability. Furthermore, proposing a programme of quantitative easing when all indicators of liquidity of the banking system are at historical maximums and short-term interest rates are at historical minimums seems completely unnecessary. To recap, the excess liquidity in Croatia exceeds the surplus liquidity in the euro area five times relative to their GDP. In addition, the CNB, unlike the ECB, has not nearly reached the limits of action through conventional measures, and there is still room for more expansionary action under the existing instrumentation. This primarily refers to the reserve requirement, which in Croatia now stands at 12%, while, by comparison, in the euro area it is only 1%. Overall, more than EUR 70 billion is currently immobilised by regulatory requirements in Croatia. liquidity kuna, or more than 20% of GDP. 1 Moreover, the loosening of these measures is not limited by additional risks to the CNB, while, for example, the ECB accumulates securities on its balance sheet by quantitative easing, thereby increasing its credit risk and raising the problem of determining the output strategy. In addition, the risks associated with the policy of quantitative easing from the creation of a bubble in financial markets, to the consequences of the long-term policy of ultra-low interest rates on the insurance and pension funds industry, are well known. It should be noted that the possible channels of action of quantitative easing on the economy in our case are superfluous, ineffective, and in some cases even dangerous. The main channel of action of quantitative easing is through the effects on the prices of financial assets. Indeed, as the ECB's benchmark short-term interest rate is already at zero level, the ECB seeks to boost domestic consumption by buying government and corporate bonds on the secondary market. The idea behind quantitative easing carried out through the purchase of bonds is to seek to act to increase prices and reduce yields on these securities, and 1 A little more than half of that amount relates to mandatory atcuvu and the rest to the minimum required foreign exchange receivables and, to a lesser extent, the obligatory cash registers of the records entered by the banks. indirectly and on the prices of other types of assets considered by investors to be substitutes and thus to a reduction in financing costs. Croatia already has indirect benefits from this channel through a decrease in the price of foreign borrowing for the state and Croatian companies. On the other hand, financing conditions in the domestic market are gradually improving anyway thanks to high liquidity, and for a significant drop in domestic interest rates, changes beyond the reach of monetary policy are necessary, and above all an improvement in the general economic climate and the perception of the riskiness of the country. The weak development of the domestic capital market and poor reliance on non-credit forms of financing further diminishes the potential effectiveness that quantitative easing policies could have on our financial assets . Finally, the exchange rate channel of quantitative easing, which is realized through the depreciation of the domestic currency, in the case of Croatia would have devastating effects on the financial stability of the country. By weakening the euro on global foreign exchange markets, the ECB seeks to limit deflationary pressures due to rising import prices expressed in other currencies, primarily the dollar. In fact, so far, the action through the exchange rate channel is more pronounced than the channel of the change in the prices of financial assets. However, in Croatia, the stable exchange rate of the kuna against the euro as a nominal anchor of monetary policy is the basis of financial stability in the country and the realization of our mandate to maintain price stability. For well-known reasons, above all the extremely high level of euroization of the Croatian economy and the high level of indebtedness in euros, the depreciation of the exchange rate as a channel of activity of quantitative dismissal is out of the question in our country. The best example of the effects of depreciation is the recent strengthening of the Swiss franc, which has shown in a painful way how exchange rate risks can materialize in the form of an increase in the burden of repayment of debts expressed in foreign exchange. The effect of the depreciation of the kuna against the euro would have many times more devastating effects. In conclusion, the European Central Bank's quantitative easing programme could generally have a positive impact on the Croatian economy. This is primarily about improving financing conditions in the euro market, and perhaps at a later stage, if this effect is dependent on monetary policy and the growth of foreign demand from the euro area. At the same time, its introduction does not require any changes in monetary policy implemented by the CNB, which has been extremely expansionary for many years. 4. Interest rate formation and country risk Although the fall in interest rates in Croatia was in some cases even more pronounced than in euro area2, their level is still over 2 percentage points higher than in the euro area (Figure 17). This confirms that the formation of interest rates depends not only on the monetary environment on which central banks operate (inter alia through regulatory cost), but also on other factors such as the cost of the source of funds (interest paid by banks on deposits and other sources), the riskiness of placements, operating cost, and ultimately earnings (Figure 18). While most of these factors have acted on falling interest rates in the recent period, the premium to cover risk remains high and has not decreased significantly. In addition to the riskiness of each individual client, this premium also seeks to cover the risk of the country in which businesses and the population are attributable. Figure 17. This risk is directly reflected in the country's credit rating, and as we know, for Croatia it has deteriorated enormously in times of crisis. The correlation between the country's rating and interest rates is best seen with interest rates on short-term loans to businesses (Figure 20) and in home loans (Figure 21), and slightly weaker in consumer loans (Figure 22). In doing so, the comparison of interest rates and ratings indicates that interest rates for loans to households in Croatia are even slightly lower than the country's credit rating would imply. Impact of foreign interest rates and risks Risk premiums for European countries and banks have been reduced to almost pre-crisis levels and interest rates in the euro area are at historically low levels (Figures 23, 24 and 25). These developments are primarily the result of the ECB's expansionary monetary policy, the relatively positively assessed results of stress tests and the quality testing of banks' assets, and the economic recovery of most EU countries and the continued fiscal consolidation in the peripheral countries of the euro area. Figure 23. Key interest rates of major central banks and leading market interest rates Izvori: Fed; ESB; Bloomberg Figure 24. Movement of credit risk insurance premiums (CDS) for five-year bonds of selected emerging market countries Spring: Bloomberg Picture 25. Movement of credit risk insurance premium (CDS) for five-year bonds of selected banks Spring: Bloomberg However, the prolonged period of exceptionally mild conditions in financial markets due to the current abundance of liquidity results in an increased risk of excessive risk-taking, which is manifested by the rise in the prices of financial assets while reducing risk premiums to levels potentially not justified by the funds. In the event of an external shock, such as the materialisation of geopolitical risks associated with developments in Ukraine and the Middle East, unexpected changes in the monetary policy of the world's leading central banks or the adverse outcome of the EU-Greece negotiations, there could be a resurgence of significant tightening of financing conditions in financial markets, risk premiums and borrowing costs adversely affected countries with pronounced external imbalances, among which Croatia stands out in particular. The CNB has been warning about this risk for some time (FS13, FS14). Namely, despite the decrease in global risk aversion and the trend of decreasing risk premiums for most countries, Croatia continues to rebound negatively from comparable countries at its height. The most important reasons for Croatia's unfavourable perception of risk are the high level of foreign debt, fast-growing public debt, the lack of economic recovery and the associated slow fiscal consolidation, as well as the postponement of structural reforms that undermine the credibility of economic policy. Due to vulnerabilities in the domestic economy, the growth of interest rates on the world market significantly affects the cost of financing the state, i.e. the interest allocation on government debt - the so-called snowball effect. 6th Snowball effect Government expenditure on interest (in % of GDP) has increased significantly over the past few years and is approaching 4% of GDP. Today, only Italy, Greece, Ireland and Hungary have higher levels of interest expenditure in the European Union. Such developments reflect an increase in the level of public debt, while at the same time the average cost of borrowing has decreased, due to the external factors mentioned above. In the medium term, however, interest rates are expected to rise in the global financial market, which will intensify adverse trends. In such a situation, fiscal adjustment will be further hampered and the anticyclical action of fiscal policy will be prevented. Figure 28. Interest expenses of the general government sector Note: The data for 2014 for Croatia is not fully comparable to previous years. Source: AMECO Furthermore, the change in interest rates affects the relative indebtedness of the state through the so-called snowball effect. snowball effect). The effect of snowballs stems from the interaction between the differential of the interest rate on debt and economic growth on the one hand and the level of public debt (in % of GDP) on the other. If the aforementioned differential is positive, as it is in the case of Croatia, the trajectory of public debt will be unsustainable (explosive) even if the sector of the state does not generate deficits. Analysis of fiscal developments shows that the impact of snowballs can explain almost half of the increase in public debt over the past six-year period, and the same effect will largely determine the dynamics of public debt in the coming period (Figure 29). A simple account best demonstrates the severity of the current situation even without changing interest rates in the global financial market. Namely, in order to stop the growth of public debt approaching the level of 90% of GDP, Croatia would have to achieve a cumulative primary surplus of over 7% of GDP, or about 25 billion euros, by the end of 2017. marten. The simulation of an increase in the implicit interest rate on new debts by 1 percentage point by 2017 increases this amount by about EUR 4 billion. marten. Current projections, however, suggest that a cumulative primary deficit of around EUR 10bn could be generated by 2017. marten. The adverse impact of snowballs on public debt dynamics could increase further by 2020, with a one percentage point increase if interest rates rise by one percentage point, it would cumulatively increase from the baseline scenario by almost EUR 14.0 billion. marten. In this way, the state can influence the decrease in the perception of riskiness of the country and higher GDP growth, thereby mitigating the impact of the growth of benchmark interest rates, the movement of which is beyond its control.
