In 2014, there was a significant decrease in loans to public companies, due to the deleveraging of three large public companies, and a slight growth in loans to private companies, while the household sector continues to deleverage, that is, it has continuously recorded a negative rate of credit growth. Total financing of the company - which includes total domestic (with credit institutions, leasing and HBOR) and foreign financing of enterprises - has grown again in the first eight months of this year, following a decline last year of 1.8 percent (again entirely caused by the deleveraging of several large public companies). It is interesting to note that private enterprises have not deleveraging in any year, that is, they continuously have a positive rate of loan growth. Credit activity is lower than would be the case in a situation of recovery, i.e. positive GDP growth. The main reason for low credit activity is the lack of demand, the second reason is the tightening of banks' credit conditions due to the increase in poor placements, both related to the weak general economic outlook in the country, the third is the lack of equity financing. In simple terms, companies can be divided: 1 All presented annual rates of change are corrected for exchange rate movements, shipyard debt acquisition, conversion of debt to capital, transfer of NPLs, bankruptcy Centre Bank d.d. methodological change in the posting of fees. - those to whom everyone would lend, but they do not want loans, because they have enough money of their own - those that come out of pre-bankruptcy settlements - these need equity investments first, and only then loans. Active equity in Croatia, however, has relatively little, the potential is partially discouraged by negative experiences from pre-bankruptcy settlements, and foreign ones have yet to be attracted. International financial institutions can also play a significant role in this, which should move more boldly from classic credit financing towards equity investments and thus serve as a catalyst for private equity, especially in smaller markets. - small and medium-sized enterprises that have a problem of lack of equity and collateral again , and banks, on the other hand, rarely finance projects based only on the projected cash flow - and to so-called start-ups, i.e. new companies looking for founding capital, i.e. someone willing to share the risk from the beginning, the so-called venture capital, which in Croatia also has very little and where again international financial institutions can play an important role as catalysts with the involvement of relatively small amounts of money. Reliance only on bank lending and banks' post-crisis risk aversion make the financing horizon relatively narrow, especially for those activities that should be encouraged the most, namely innovation and technological investment. In addition to the aforementioned role of international financial institutions, there is also room for state intervention. EU funds can be used for leverage for international financial institutions and then private capital, with multiple positive effects on the availability of financing where it is currently most needed. Subsidies in Croatia are high in relation to GDP and to other EU countries, but there is no assessment of the effectiveness of these subsidies. In the high degree of arbitrariness of subsidy decisions, which lasts for decades, without serious analysis, does the state fail to encourage potentially propulsive sectors of more added value through subsidies? Does this lose GDP growth? On the other hand, banks live primarily on loans. If their interest income falls, this is due not only to the spoiling of the loan portfolio, but also to reduce it. It is in the interests of banks to increase placements, especially since newer loans are of better quality than older years. The largest number of non-performing bank loans dates back to the year before the start of the crisis, when loans were handed out with a fist and a cap. The focus on managing that part of the portfolio - on the past - usually causes insufficient focus on future revenues. The key, of course, is the allocation of loans, but not only loans but capital in general, including equity. A large number of domestic entrepreneurs missed out on the 'golden' time of the capital market in the mid-2000s for capital increases, i.e. for equity financing, rather than through debt. A lot of people got their revenge later. Debt turned out to be a bad comrade, worse than those they wanted to avoid, rejecting the possibility of recapitalization through the issuance of share capital. Due to continued deleveraging, i.e. the reduction of debt to banks and the growth of assets in banks and non-bank financial institutions, the net financial wealth of the household sector increased by over 75% compared to 2009. year. Personal consumption, along with the decline in investments, represents the most significant negative contribution to domestic demand and therefore to the development of GDP. It is often misinterpreted that fiscal consolidation policy has contributed to the fall in GDP, but cumulatively, in the last five years, it has not had a negative impact on the fall in GDP. However, it is required by the process of the EDP (excessive deficit procedures) in which the Republic of Croatia entered last year. Table 2. It is low primarily due to the state of the labour market, i.e. the continuous job cuts due to lack of investment. As long as the prospects of losing employment outweigh the prospect of gaining employment, it is difficult to expect a significant recovery in personal consumption. Figure 3. Consumer Spending Index Standardized values, three-member moving averages, Sources: Ipsos Puls, HNB This leads us to conclude that the fundamental precondition for economic recovery in Croatia is the increase in investments. If it occurs, it will be quickly followed by a recovery in personal consumption, since the net financial wealth of the population sector is significantly better than it was five years ago. The increase in investment and personal spending will more than compensate for the negative contribution of public spending to economic growth, which will be present in the next few years due to fiscal consolidation within the EDP procedure. However, gradual GDP growth will also allow for less social pain due to fiscal consolidation. In other words, from a negative spiral, the economy can, relatively quickly, go from positive. But investments must precede everything else. Investments have had the biggest impact on the fall in GDP in the last 5 years - cumulatively 9.1 %. The fundamental question of the recovery of economic growth in Croatia is therefore: what is needed to finally start investments? I've been saying this for years, and unfortunately, I can't be innovative this time either - structural reforms are necessary to improve the business and investment climate. This time, in support of this argument, I can add, in addition to the analyses so far, the figures of the OECD, which, for the first time, for 2013 included Croatia in its comparative analysis. Structural reforms according to the OECD Product Market Regulation Index between 2008 and 2013 For the first time, Croatia was included in the OECD report for 2013, recording a very poor product market regulation index or, for short, PMR) of 2.08 above (less favourable than) the average of OECD countries (1.47) in the year under review and the EU27 average of the countries surveyed (1.42). All central and eastern European countries surveyed recorded lower PMR values in 2013, i.e. on average they have a lower level of product market regulation than Croatia. Figure 4 PMR Index of EU countries Izvor: OECD The most favourable pmr indicator values in 2013 compared to the average of EU countries, Croatia achieves in the field of removing barriers to entrepreneurship, while noticeably negatively deviating in the field of removing barriers to trade and investment, especially in removing barriers to foreign direct investment, where it stands significantly worse than all the other countries surveyed by the analysis. Deregulation is key to unleashing and fostering entrepreneurial spirit. Too much regulation, too many regulations, demands, bureaucracy, levies at all levels, from state to local, take up time, energy and money that can be used much better. Or, worse, it distracts people from entrepreneurship, and therefore from creating jobs and increasing GDP. The deregulation initiative is useful to leave it to the entrepreneurs themselves, but it is demanding primarily because it requires a team of highly skilled and well-motivated people at the state administration level to analyse and translate their initiatives into reducing regulation. Capital and work (education) For decades, the settled income divide, where about two-thirds or 70% of GDP belonged to labour and about a third belonged to capital, is changing rapidly, so today's estimates suggest that this division in more developed countries has fallen to just 55%:45% in favour of labour. Capital gradually substitutes work. For the future of the country and the design of the education system, it is extremely important to take into account that we may be witnessing bifurcation in the labor market, as recent research suggests. The state, as by far the largest investor in this sector, should carefully evaluate the efficiency of investments in this segment and design the education system based on the analytical basis of the assessment of demand in the labor market. The appropriate policy must increase the efficiency of education, which according to the results of PISA tests, as well as according to the ranking of domestic universities is low, unsatisfactory. The quality of education and the non-compliance of the education system with the needs of the labour market leads to and will lead to a loss of competitiveness due to the lack of staff with adequate knowledge and skills on the one hand, and to the dissatisfaction of the population due to the inability to find jobs consistent with their knowledge and skills on the other. The experience of countries such as Germany, Austria or Switzerland shows that vocational education and practice help facilitate employment in the labour market after school. On the other hand, experience shows that if young people fail to get involved in the labour market relatively early after finishing school, their human capital depreciates quite quickly and they are often doomed to long-term unemployment. Political economy The political framework for implementing the necessary structural reforms, however, remains unchanged. And after six years of recession, the entire domestic political spectrum is dominated by the short-term goal of easily winning votes, over the goal of creating an efficient, open, flexible economy, which is able to generate enough jobs. In this, even the structure of the political system in which almost every year the elections are almost every year certainly does not help.

Title: Bankers are reluctantly under the stage lights
text: HPVATRKA ON THE MORNING Bankers are reluctantly under the spotlight Published: 15/12/2023 Column by Governor Boris Vuji for Business Outlook/Jutarnji list, published on 15 December 2023 Jon Postel, the late American computer scientist, the man who took care of the Internet domain name system, and was considered by some to be the reason closest to the status of the "god of the Internet", he concluded that the stage lights have their minuses. I'm sure banks are well aware of this. The CNB collects their financial reports and publishes business results at a frequent and predictable pace. The media have adapted to this rhythm, so every quarter they eagerly await a new announcement, and commentators analyze it in detail, including a discussion about the desirability and justification of the achievements Results. On the other hand, business in the rest of the economy mostly takes place in the deep shadows. The media's interest is much smaller. True, companies that are listed on the stock exchange publish their financial statements. For them, as well as for other companies, the Financial Agency collects and publishes business results once a year, usually in the second half of the following year. However, the publication of banks' financial indicators is characterised by a unique A combination of comprehensiveness, timeliness and easy access. Therefore, companies in industries that are often noticeably more profitable than banks are very successful in avoiding the hot lights of the stage, from which bankers cannot escape, and which cause them discomfort today. The cause of the current discomfort of banks across Europe is the growth of profits to the levels they last recorded on the eve of the global financial crisis. The financial indicators of domestic banks followed the general developments. Moreover, given the generous liquidity surpluses created by many years of efforts to prevent the appreciation of the kuna exchange rate, they were also better positioned than most European banks to take advantage of the cycle of interest rate growth to increase revenues. The growth in interest income of domestic banks was thus mostly generated by a high share of short-term assets that are sensitive to interest rate increases, mainly in the form of deposits with the central bank. Revenues from lending to the government increased to a lesser extent, reflecting higher yields on government bonds, and revenues from corporate lending also increased somewhat. On the other hand, and contrary to the widely held perception, in the first three quarters of this year, the cost of interest paid by banks on household deposits increased more than their income from interest on household loans. This is not the case in most other EU countries and is a consequence of the consumer protection that the CNB and the Government have been implementing for the last ten years. Thus, primarily thanks to the return on risk-free overnight assets, within the ECB's new monetary policy framework, banks reached a return on equity of almost 17 percent at the end of September. This is a truly impressive level of profitability, and the news about it has recently gone through all portals. However, it is less known to the public that last year's return on capital in information and communication activities was close to that level, and in trade it even exceeded it - and in a year when the return on capital of banks was around 8 percent, they easily seem like "money factories" at first, which in a figurative sense they really are. It is true that banks are generally miles away from the profitability indicators recorded by some other industries. Has the new period of elevated interest rates restored to banks the "Midin touch" they had before the global financial crisis? Will the new period of elevated interest rates and high profitability of banks last? And will it lead to a new financial crisis? Investors and analysts are not overly optimistic about the sustainability of banks' elevated profits for now. Despite record business results, the share prices of European banks jumped only slightly. Likewise, regulators continuously warn of risks that could turn a period of high profitability into a memory of a mere A short-lived episode of banking luck. Such considerations are dominated by two groups of effects - short-term and long-term. In the short term, bankers are already seeing rising interest rates on deposits erode their profits. While interest rates on corporate time deposits reached the level of 3 percent a few months ago, in October the average interest rates on new term deposits for individuals jumped from 1.5 percent in September to 2.5 percent. Since deposits have a much shorter maturity than loans, and an increase in interest rates on deposits, once it occurs, spills over to interest costs much faster than an increase in interest rates on loans can increase revenues. The relocation of deposits from current and giro accounts to term deposits further enhances the effect of rising deposit rates on interest costs. In October, the share of time deposits in total deposits of citizens increased significantly for the first time in a long time, as citizens switched approximately EUR 600 million to term deposits. If the proportion of time deposits continues to increase, it can erode profits relatively quickly, even if it does not jump from the current quarter to almost two-thirds, where it was about five years ago. Another short-term challenge for banks is the risk that higher debt servicing costs for businesses and individuals will be delayed in an increase in non-performing loans and related costs for banks. These costs are not yet rising because economic growth is very strong, unemployment is low, and businesses are doing well, making it easier for everyone to repay their loans in an orderly manner. However, in Europe, where growth is much weaker, there are already some early signs of deterioration in asset quality. If they successfully overcome short-term challenges, we must not forget that the structural problems of the banking sector have not disappeared due to short-term profit growth. Banks continue to operate in a highly regulated industry that limits the ability to take risks and consequently make profits. However, in certain segments of their business, banks are very exposed to competition from new players from the technology sector, which is probably most evident in the area of payment transactions at the moment. Banks should therefore use the period of increased profitability to continue investing in digital development, improving cost efficiency and strengthening their capital position. If it were a growing industry with great profitability prospects, you would hardly find indicators that speak of a decrease in the number of branches by about a third and the number of employees by about a seventh over a period of ten years, as shown by the indicators for domestic banks. And such a trend is likely to continue in the future, despite a temporary spike in profitability that, reluctantly, brought them back into the spotlight. CROATIAN NATIONAL BANK
text_original: HPVATRKA NAPODNA RANKA Bankari su nevoljko pod svjetlima pozornice Objavljeno: 15.12.2023. Kolumna guvernera Borisa Vujia za Business Outlook/Jutarnji list, objavljena 15. prosinca 2023. Jon Postel, pokojni ameriki informatiar, ovjek koji je vodio rauna o sustavu naziva internetskih domena, a neki su ga zbog toga smatrali najbliim statusu "boga interneta", zakljuio je da svjetla pozornice imaju svoje minuse. Toga su, siguran sam, itekako svjesne i banke. HNB estim i predvidljivim ritmom prikuplja njihova financijska izvjea i objavljuje poslovne rezultate. Mediji su se prilagodili tome ritmu pa svako tromjeseje s velikim nestrpljenjem oekuju novu objavu, a komentatori je detaljno ralanjuju, ukljuujui i raspravu o poeljnosti i opravdanosti ostvarenih rezultata. S druge strane, poslovanje u ostatku gospodarstva uglavnom se odvija u dubokoj sjeni. Interes medija je daleko manji. Istina, tvrtke koje su izlistane na burzi objavljuju svoja financijska izvjea. Za njih takoer, kao i za ostale tvrtke, Financijska agencija jednom godinje prikupi i objavi poslovne rezultate, i to obino u drugoj polovici naredne godine. Meutim, objavu financijskih pokazatelja banaka karakterizira jedinstvena kombinacija sveobuhvatnosti, aurnosti i jednostavnog pristupa. Stoga tvrtke u djelatnostima koje su esto osjetno profitabilnije od banaka vrlo uspjeno izbjegavaju vrua svjetla pozornice, od kojih bankari ne mogu pobjei, a koja im danas izazivaju nelagodu. Uzrok trenutne nelagode banaka po cijeloj Europi je rast profita do razina kakve su zadnji put biljeile jo uoi globalne financijske krize. Financijski pokazatelji domaih banaka pratili su opa kretanja. tovie, s obzirom na izdane vikove likvidnosti, stvorene dugogodinjim naporima da se sprijei jaanje teaja kune, one su bile i bolje pozicionirane od veine europskih banaka da iskoriste ciklus rasta kamatnih stopa za poveanje prihoda. Rast kamatnog prihoda domaih banaka tako je najvie generirao visok udjel kratkorone imovine koja je osjetljiva na porast kamatnih stopa, uglavnom u obliku depozita kod sredinje banke. U manjoj su mjeri porasli prihodi od kreditiranja drave, kao odraz viih prinosa na dravne obveznice, a donekle su porasli i prihodi od kreditiranja poduzea. S druge strane, i suprotno iroko uvrijeenoj percepciji, u prva tri tromjeseja ove godine bankama je vie porastao troak kamata koje su platile na depozite kuanstava, nego to su im porasli prihodi od kamata na kredite kuanstvima. To nije sluaj u veini drugih zemalja EU i posljedica je zatite potroaa koju je HNB zajedno s Vladom provodio zadnjih desetak godina. Dakle, prvenstveno zahvaljujui povratu na bezrizinu prekonono deponiranu aktivu, unutar novog okvira monetarne politike ECB-a, banke su na kraju rujna dosegnule povrat na kapital od gotovo 17 posto. To je uistinu impresivna razina profitabilnosti, a vijest o njoj nedavno je prohujala svim portalima. No, javnosti je manje poznato da je lani povrat na kapital u informacijskoj i komunikacijskoj djelatnosti bio na domak te razine, a u trgovini ju je i nadmaio - i to u godini kada se povrat na kapital banaka vrtio oko 8 posto, lako na prvu djeluju kao "tvornice novca", to u prenesenom smislu doista i jesu, istina je da su banke uglavnom miljama daleko od pokazatelja profitabilnosti koje biljee neke druge djelatnosti. Je li novo razdoblje povienih kamatnih stopa bankama povratilo "Midin dodir" koji su imali do globalne financijske krize? Hoe li novo razdoblje povienih kamata i visoke profitabilnosti banaka potrajati? I hoe li dovesti do nove financijske krize? Ulagai i analitiari za sada nisu pretjerano optimistini u pogledu odrivosti povienih profita banaka. Unato rekordnim rezultatima poslovanja, cijene dionica europskih banaka tek su blago skoile. Isto tako, regulatori kontinuirano upozoravaju na rizike koji bi razdoblje visoke profitabilnosti mogli pretvoriti u uspomenu na tek kratkotrajnu epizodu bankarske sree. U takvim razmatranjima dominiraju dvije skupine uinaka - kratkoroni i dugoroni. Kratkorono, bankari ve vide kako im sve vie kamatne stope na depozite nagrizaju profite. Dok su kamatne stope na oroene depozite poduzea jo prije nekoliko mjeseci dosegle razinu od 3 posto, u listopadu su i prosjene kamate na nova oroenja za graane skoile s 1,5 posto, koliko su bile u rujnu, na 2,5 posto. Budui da depoziti imaju znatno krae dospijee od kredita, i porast kamatnih stopa na depozite, jednom kad do njega doe, znatno se bre prelijeva na kamatne trokove nego to rast kamatnih stopa na kredite moe poveati prihode. Selidba depozita s tekuih i iro rauna na oroenja dodatno pojaava uinak rasta depozitnih stopa na kamatne trokove. U listopadu je tako udjel oroenih u ukupnim depozitima graana osjetno porastao po prvi put u due vremena budui da su graani prebacili na oroenja otprilike 600 milijuna eura. Ako se udjel oroenih depozita nastavi poveavati, to moe relativno brzo nagristi dobit, ak i ako ne skoi s trenutne etvrtine na gotovo dvije treine, gdje je bio prije otprilike pet godina. Drugi kratkoroni izazov za banke predstavlja rizik da se vii trokovi servisiranja duga za poduzea i graane s vremenskom odgodom odraze na porast neprihodujuih kredita i povezanih trokova za banke. Ti trokovi za sada jo ne rastu jer je gospodarski rast vrlo snaan, nezaposlenost je niska, a poduzea dobro posluju, to svima olakava urednu otplatu kredita. No, u Europi, gdje je rast kudikamo slabiji, ve su vidljive odreene rane naznake kvarenja kvalitete imovine. Ako se uspjeno othrvaju kratkoronim izazovima, ne smijemo zaboraviti ni da strukturni problemi bankarskog sektora nisu nestali zbog kratkoronog rasta profita. Banke i dalje posluju u visoko reguliranoj industriji koja ograniava mogunost preuzimanja rizika i posljedino zarade. No, u pojedinim su segmentima poslovanja banke itekako izloene konkurenciji novih igraa iz tehnolokog sektora, to je trenutno vjerojatno najoitije u podruju platnog prometa. Razdoblje poviene profitabilnosti banke bi stoga trebale iskoristiti za nastavak ulaganja u digitalni razvoj, poboljanje trokovne uinkovitosti i jaanje kapitalne pozicije. Da se radi o rastuoj industriji s velikim perspektivama profitabilnosti teko da biste pronali pokazatelje koji govore o smanjenju broja poslovnica za otprilike treinu i broja zaposlenih za otprilike sedminu kroz razdoblje od desetak godina, kao to to pokazuju pokazatelji za domae banke. A takav e se trend vjerojatno nastaviti i u budunosti, unato privremenom skoku profitabilnosti koji ih je, nevoljko, vratio pod sjaj svjetala pozornice.  HRVATSKA NARODNA BANKA

Title: The cost of fighting inflation: unacceptable or inevitable?
text: HPVATRKA ON THE MORNING The price of fighting inflation: unacceptable or inevitable? Published: 23/8/2023 In a column for the weekly Nacional, published on 22 August 2023, Deputy Governor Sandra svaljek explains the side effects of monetary policy tightening. The fact that central banks are now paying large amounts to commercial banks while commercial banks keep interest rates low on their customers' deposits seems like an unfair side effect of the fight against inflation. Should such a situation be corrected - if not by monetary policy measures, then by tax or some other economic policy measures Descriptions of the modalities of monetary policy implementation are not fun reading, especially in the summer. However, when they become controversial and provoke media and professional attention and reactions of politicians, become a topic that needs to be shed light on and contribute to its understanding. Currently, this status has been earned by the interest that euro area commercial banks receive on funds deposited with central banks, which is one of the reasons for the significant growth in their total income and profits. As of mid-2022. The European Central Bank, determined to lower the inflation rate to the target level of 2 percent in due course, is tightening monetary policy sharply, primarily by raising key interest rates - the interest rate on overnight deposits, the interest rate on main refinancing operations and the interest rate on the marginal lending facility. At nine consecutive meetings of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank, the interest rate on cash deposits was raised from -0.5% to 3.75%, or by 425 basis points. Due to large surpluses liquidity of commercial banks deposited in their accounts with central banks, such an increase has resulted in significant interest payments euro area banks and, as a rule, growth in their total income and profits. Such a side effect of implementing monetary policy with the aim of suppressing inflation is considered by many to be unjustified subsidies to commercial banks, which has raised a number of questions, especially in the light of expectations of a prolonged period of poor financial results of central banks. Here are the answers to some of them. Why do central banks pay interest on bank reserves? Central banks began to pay interest on commercial bank funds deposited with them in order to improve the effectiveness of monetary policy. Interest rates on deposits, as well as on loans to commercial banks, Central banks influence the level of all other interest rates and the prices of various forms of assets. The main objective of central banks is to maintain price stability, not to make a profit. Losses are not an obstacle for them Is the payment of interest on excess liquidity of commercial banks a feature of the Eurosystem or a standard element of modern monetary policy frameworks? The Eurosystem has been paying interest on commercial banks' excess liquidity since its inception in 1999, the US Federal Reserve introduced this practice in 2008, and is now used by the Bank of England, the Bank of Japan and most central banks. However, interest payments to commercial banks have been low so far and therefore have not attracted attention. Until 2008, the liquidity of commercial banks was scarce and there was no accumulation of liquidity surpluses commercial banks in their accounts with central banks. At a time when large asset purchase programmes to support the post-global financial crisis recovery have created an abundance of liquidity surpluses, interest rates on cash deposits have fallen significantly. In the In the euro area, interest rates were equal to or below zero over the ten-year period from 2012 to 2022. In other words, although the payment of interest to commercial banks on their reserves was part of the monetary framework, these payments de facto did not occur. Why has the payment of interest on commercial banks' reserves become particularly important now? Since the global financial crisis, central banks' monetary policies have been continuously in the function of supporting economic growth and combating extremely low and even negative inflation rates, which has been achieved through low interest rates and asset purchases, as well as various bank financing programmes under extremely favourable conditions. Bank liquidity was therefore growing, and the onset of inflation in 2021 found the banking system in a regime of exceptional liquidity abundance. In such circumstances, the interest rate on commercial banks' cash deposits in their central bank accounts became the basic monetary policy instrument, rather than the interest rate on bank borrowing with central banks. Since it defines earnings from passive holding of liquidity, banks, along with other factors, take it into account in decisions on the active management of these funds, i.e. on lending. It is estimated that by the end of the year, the CNB will pay out about EUR 460 million in interest to commercial banks, and about EUR 80 million to the state What does the payment of interest to banks mean for the financial result of central banks and their ability to achieve legal goals? It is not difficult to conclude that tightening monetary policy by raising the interest rate on banks' cash deposits is costly for central banks, i.e. that it significantly increases central banks' costs and leads to a drop in profits and possibly losses for central banks. The main goal of central banks, however, is to maintain price stability, not to make a profit. Given their specific role, financial losses and even a complete loss of capital are not an obstacle for central banks to operate and perform their legal tasks. Moreover, in times of crisis such as the period of elevated inflation, central banks' losses are justified if they are an inevitable consequence of policies aimed at combating inflation. What does the reduction in central bank profits mean for taxpayers? A decline in profits or losses of central banks means that central banks will allocate significantly lower amounts to the state budget this year, and possibly in the years to come, or will not make a profit at all that they could transfer to the budget. However, this does not necessarily mean that central banks will not contribute to filling the state budget. Namely, countries can also earn interest on funds deposited with euro area central banks at a rate that cannot currently be less than 0 or higher than the STR interbank interest rate minus 20 basis points, whereby each central bank can choose the interest rate within the limits defined in this way to apply to government deposits. Most central banks, including the Croatia National Bank, charge interest on funds in state accounts at the highest permitted interest rate, which today is around 3.45 percent. It is estimated that by the end of the year, the Croatia National Bank will pay out around EUR 460 million in interest to commercial banks. Government revenues based on interest will be significantly lower, but could amount to between EUR 80 and 90 million, which is an amount that exceeds last year's amount of the CNB's profit distribution to the state budget. In times of crisis, such as periods of elevated inflation, central bank losses are justified if they are an inevitable consequence of policies aimed at fighting inflation Should other economic policy measures correct the consequences of "subsidizing" banks? The fact that central banks pay large sums to commercial banks, while commercial banks maintain low interest rates on their customers' deposits, acts as an unfair redistribution of wealth that should be corrected, if not by monetary policy measures, then by tax or other economic policy measures. However, when considering the introduction (or, in the case of Croatia, the continuation of the application) of an additional tax on banks, account should also be taken of the fact that such a tax should be carefully designed so as not to provoke undesirable market reactions or adversely affect financial stability if it ignores that rising interest rates lead to an increase in banks' credit risk and related costs. Moreover, as much as the payment of interest on the funds of commercial banks in their accounts with central banks appears to be a negative consequence of monetary policy, the question is whether its correction is necessary, given that the financial results of central banks will gradually recover. What can be learned from this episode? Regardless of the moves of other economic policy makers, central banks will draw lessons for the future from the episode of a sudden turn in monetary policy. One reason is potentially negative side effects such as large interest payments banks, and secondly, the fact that the implementation of an asset purchase programme to support growth on a continuous basis also implies an obligation to apply it in the long term, and such an obligation cannot be fulfilled if circumstances change unexpectedly. In a new implementation cycle accommodative monetary policy, central banks are likely to be more cautious about the volume and length of the implementation of the quantitative easing programme. easing and increasing banks' liquidity reserves. text_original: HPVATRKA NAPODNA RANKA Cijena borbe protiv inflacije: neprihvatljiva ili neizbjena? Objavljeno: 23.8.2023. U kolumni za tjednik Nacional, objavljenoj 22. kolovoza 2023., zamjenica guvernera Sandra valjek objanjava popratne posljedice pootravanja monetarne politike. injenica da sredinje banke sada plaaju velike iznose poslovnim bankama dok poslovne banke zadravaju niske kamatne stope na depozite svojih klijenata, djeluje poput nepravedne popratne pojave borbe protiv inflacije. Treba li takvu situaciju ispraviti - ako ne mjerama monetarne politike, onda mjerama porezne ili neke druge ekonomske politike Opisi modaliteta provedbe monetarne politike nisu zabavno tivo, osobito ljeti. No, kada postanu kontroverzni te izazovu medijsku i strunu pozornost te reakcije politiara, postaju tema koju treba rasvijetliti i pridonijeti njezinu razumijevanju. Trenutano su takav status zavrijedile kamate koje poslovne banke u europodruju primaju na sredstva poloena kod sredinjih banaka, to je jedan od razloga znaajnog rasta njihovih ukupnih prihoda i profita. Od sredine 2022. Europska sredinja banka, odluna u namjeri da spusti stopu inflacije na ciljnu razinu od 2 posto u primjerenom roku, provodi snano pootravanje monetarne politike ponajprije diui kljune kamatne stope - kamatnu stopu na prekonone depozite, kamatnu stopu na glavne operacije refinanciranja i kamatnu stopu na mogunost posudbe na kraju dana. Na devet uzastopnih sastanaka Upravnog vijea Europske sredinje banke kamatna stopa na novane depozite podignuta je s -0,5 na 3,75 %, odnosno za 425 baznih bodova. Zbog velikih vikova likvidnosti poslovnih banaka deponiranih na njihovim raunima kod sredinjih banaka, takav je porast rezultirao znatnim plaanjima kamata bankama europodruja i u pravilu rastom njihovih ukupnih prihoda i profita. Takvu popratnu posljedicu provedbe monetarne politike s ciljem guenja inflacije mnogi smatraju neopravdanim subvencioniranjem poslovnih banaka, to je otvorilo brojna pitanja, osobito u svjetlu oekivanja duljeg razdoblja loih financijskih rezultata sredinjih banaka. Ovdje su odgovori na neka od njih. Zato sredinje banke plaaju kamate na rezerve banaka? Sredinje banke poele su plaati kamate na sredstva poslovnih banaka deponirana kod njih kako bi pospjeile djelotvornost monetarne politike. Kamatnim stopama na depozite, kao i onima na kredite poslovnim bankama, sredinje banke utjeu na visinu svih ostalih kamatnih stopa i cijene razliitih oblika imovine. Osnovni je cilj djelovanja sredinjih banaka ouvanje stabilnosti cijena, a ne ostvarivanje profita. Gubici im nisu prepreka Je li plaanje kamata na vikove likvidnosti poslovnih banaka posebnost Eurosustava ili standardni element suvremenih okvira monetarne politike? Eurosustav plaa kamate na vikove likvidnosti poslovnih banaka od svog nastanka 1999., amerike Federalne rezerve tu su praksu uvele 2008., a danas je primjenjuju i Bank of England, Bank of Japan i veina sredinjih banaka. No isplate kamata poslovnim bankama sve do sada bile su niske te samim time nisu privlaile pozornost. Do 2008. likvidnost poslovnih banaka bila je oskudna i nije postojalo kumuliranje vikova likvidnosti poslovnih banaka na njihovim raunima kod sredinjih banaka. U razdoblju kada su programi velikog otkupa vrijednosnih papira radi potpore oporavku poslije globalne financijske krize stvorili obilje vikova likvidnosti, kamatne stope na novane depozite znatno su smanjene. U europodruju su kamatne stope u desetogodinjem razdoblju od 2012. do 2022. bile jednake ili manje od nule. Drugim rijeima, iako je plaanje kamata poslovnim bankama na njihove rezerve bilo dio monetarnog okvira, te se isplate de facto nisu dogaale. Zato je plaanje kamata na rezerve poslovnih banaka sada postalo osobito vano? Monetarne politike sredinjih banaka od globalne financijske krize naovamo kontinuirano su bile u funkciji podrke gospodarskom rastu i suzbijanja iznimno niskih pa i negativnih stopa inflacije, a to se postizalo niskim kamatnim stopama i otkupom vrijednosnih papira te razliitim programima financiranja banaka uz iznimno povoljne uvjete. Likvidnost banaka stoga je rasla te je pojava inflacije 2021. zatekla bankovni sustav u reimu iznimnog obilja likvidnosti. U takvim je okolnostima osnovni instrument monetarne politike postala kamatna stopa na novane depozite poslovnih banaka na njihovim raunima u sredinjim bankama, a ne kamatna stopa na zaduivanje banaka kod sredinjih banaka. Budui da ona definira zaradu od pasivnog dranja likvidnosti, banke je, s drugim faktorima, uzimaju u obzir u odlukama o aktivnom upravljanju tim sredstvima, odnosno o kreditiranju. Procjenjuje se da e do kraja godine HNB poslovnim bankama isplatiti oko 460 milijuna eura na osnovi kamata, a dravi oko 80 to plaanje kamata bankama znai za financijski rezultat sredinjih banaka i njihovu sposobnost ostvarivanja zakonskih ciljeva? Nije teko zakljuiti da je pootravanje monetarne politike podizanjem kamatne stope na novane depozite banaka skupo za sredinje banke, odnosno da ono znatno poveava trokove sredinjih banaka i dovodi do pada dobiti, a moda i do gubitaka sredinjih banaka. Osnovni je cilj djelovanja sredinjih banaka, meutim, ouvanje stabilnosti cijena, a ne ostvarivanje profita. S obzirom na njihovu specifinu ulogu, financijski gubici pa ak i potpuni gubitak kapitala nisu prepreka sredinjim bankama za poslovanje i obavljanje zakonskih zadaa. tovie, u vremenima kriza kakvo je i razdoblje poviene inflacije, gubici su sredinjih banaka opravdani ako su nastali kao neizbjena posljedica politike usmjerene borbi protiv inflacije. to smanjenje dobiti sredinje banke znai poreznim obveznicima? Pad dobiti ili gubitak sredinjih banaka znai da e sredinje banke ove, a moda i sljedeih godina, u dravni proraun raspodjeljivati znatno nie iznose ili uope nee ostvariti dobit koju bi mogle prenijeti u proraun. Title: Climate change requires a deep, structural transformation of all sectors.
text: HPVATRk'A NAPODNA RANKA Climate change requires deep, structural transformation of every sector Published: 4/10/2022 Speech by Deputy Governor Sandra Svaljek at Startup Europe Regatta 2022 on 4 October2022. In 2010, I have spent ten days in Japan, participating in Japanese government's programme called Partnership for 21st century. Back then, Japan was engaged in compiling country's long-term strategy of which I have learned quite a lot, visiting several ministries, corporations and research institutes. Like most strategic documents, Japanese strategy identified current strengths and weaknesses, as well as future threats and opportunities. There was a widespread understanding that decline in population size and the ensuing ageing of the population is one of the major threats to country's future growth. However, to my surprise, it was at the same time considered a great opportunity, bringing a potential for the rise in demand for elderly care, robotics, mobile health services, electric appliances and housing adapted to the needs of elderly. It is then that I have discovered a unique but powerful philosophy, according to which the inconvenient circumstances should not be considered as curse, but could be embraced and turned into building blocks of progress. The world we live in is characterized by many challenges, one of them being climate crisis, which is lately showing in many different forms - heatwaves, floods, droughts, wildfires, hurricanes and unprecedented storms. Human activity and the way we use the natural resources have devastating consequences for the planet. According to the Stockholm resilience centre, four of nine planetary boundaries have been crossed and large, irreversible changes might soon become unavoidable. Accumulation of greenhouse gasses in the atmosphere, causing climate change is one of them. Global community is therefore united in a determination to prevent global temperatures to rise more than 1,5 degrees Celsius above the preindustrial levels. Growth of global temperatures by 1,5 degrees is consistent with the level of CO2 in the atmosphere of 2.700 Gt (this is often called carbon budget), and there are already 2.400 Gt of the excess CO2 in the atmosphere. With the current annual emissions, the carbon budget will be reached in only 8 years. In other words, if 2.700 Gt would be one hour, we would have exactly 7 minutes to stop emitting and prevent rise in temperatures by more than 1,5 degrees. This to my opinion is a major wake up call. But (equipped with my Japanese experience), I would as well considered this is as one of the greatest opportunities of all times. Climate change requires deep, structural transformation of every single sector of the entire economy - from farming to transportation, from how we produce shoes and clothes, to how we build and warm up our houses. No business will stay unaffected by this change - the incumbent business will have to adapt, pressured by the expectations of their employees, customers and investors to take steps towards incorporating climate and environmental concerns into their businessmaking. At the same time, many new business may arise as well, stimulated by the demand for sustainable products and services and a hunger for decarbonizing solutions. Interestingly, it is proved that start-ups have been the first to scale-up so-called climate tech business, like renewable energy and electric vehicles. The state of the environment is surely worrying; however, the prospects for economic prosperity are not grim. We know that there are already technological solutions available, which could be profitable, and have great abatement potential. Technologies such as solar power, wind power, food waste technology, green hydrogen production and alternative foods have the potential to reduce GHG emissions by 80 percent. New business reaping the potential of such technologies could nowadays receive external funding from financial institutions across the risk spectrum - from green angel investors and green venture capitalists, to institutional investors and banks. According to McKinsey, investing in climate tech (businesses in the area of renewable energy, electric vehicles, carbon removal, food waste, agriculture and the decarbonisation of the built environment) already accounts for 1/8 of all VC investments. In 2021 there were 78 unicorns across eight climate tech challenge areas. The intensity and speed of development of digital economy we saw in recent decades might be followed by the equal development in decarbonisation economy. Banks as well are prone to including the financing of sustainable projects into their lending portfolio. Since 2017 central banks have been agile in rising banks' awareness of the climate and environmental risks they have been exposed to. The latest climate stress test carried out by the ECB on 104 European significant banks showed their overreliance on carbon-emitting sectors - almost two-thirds of banks income from non-financial corporate customers stems from greenhouse gas-intensive industries. In the future, the banks may therefore intend to restructure their portfolio and replace gradually the loans to carbon intensive sectors with loans to sustainable business and thus lower their exposure to climate risks. At the end, let me encourage those of you that are considering starting up a climate-tech business or having already established a business in this area - I am very exciting about what the future brings to you. As I see it, there are all the important ingredients for your success. There is a growing demand for sustainable products and services, there are various policy measures implemented by the governments in order to support decarbonisation, there are already available profitable new technologies and there is an appetite of the financial sector to provide financing. Make use of the climate crisis, and in the same time make our planet healthier! CROATIAN NATIONAL BANK

Title: Croatian road to the euro: Test driving the new ERM II setup
text: HPVATRk'A NAPODNA RANKA Croatian road to the euro: Test driving the new ERM II setup Published: 29/9/2022 Article by Governor Vujcic for Obserwator Finansowy, 27th September, 2022 A quip on Balkans producing more history than it can consume, famously but incorrectly attributed to Churchill, is a good description of the Croatian history towards the end of the 20th century. However, at the turn of the century, Croatia managed to escape "Churchill's curse" in a quest to become a "boring" country with a negligible footprint on global affairs. With the clock to the euro introduction resolutely ticking, Croatia is once again starting to appear in the headlines of international press. And collective hopes and anxieties of the West - or at least some part of it - are again refracted through the lens of the Croatian experience. This time round, the euro adoption in Croatia encouraged some commentators to announce the build-up of an even stronger momentum for further EU integration. On the other hand, it is also stoking public fears that the enlargement could further exacerbate the risk of euro area fragmentation. Also, some are probably waiting on the side-lines to learn from the outcome of this ..natural experiment. My goal for this text is to provide all these people with our own optics on the euro adoption - to describe why it has always made sense for Croatia to pursue a speedy euro introduction, to elaborate on the Croatian path to the euro area membership and finally, to provide a first account of the successful completion of participation in the newly set up ERM II framework. Bob Dylan probably did not spare much thought about monetary policy when composing his timeless hit Like a Rolling Stone. Yet, few accounts of monetary policy frameworks in small open economies are as accurate as his assertion that When you aint got nothing, you got nothing to lose. For Croatia, one of the small EU member states (indeed, Croatia is at the moment the smallest one outside the euro area), highly euroized and deeply integrated into the euro area in terms of trade and finance, the most important monetary policy decisions had been made in Frankfurt even long before the creation of the euro. As monetary policy has for almost three decades been geared towards the stabilization of the exchange rate against the euro, it has never acquired more than a very few degrees of freedom. Indeed, during the crisis periods, the exchange rate played the role of a shock amplifier rather than a shock absorber envisaged in standard macro textbooks. The rush of firms and households to convert their local currency holdings into euros at the very first sign of a crisis has always threatened to quickly turn upside down any monetary accommodation in the crisis environment. In order to maintain monetary and financial stability in such an environment, the central bank relied on a broad spectrum of macroprudential proto-tools, applied in an integrated fashion with the monetary policy. But ample prudential buffers were costly for the financial system, while maintaining a stable exchange rate diminished the potential benefits of having an own currency. The euro introduction has provided an exit strategy from a monetary arrangement saddled with all the costs associated with participation in the monetary union, but very few of the benefits accruing to members of the monetary union. For all these reasons, joining the euro-area has been a long-time goal for Croatia. However, by mid-2013, when the belated EU accession took place, the echoes of the sovereign debt crisis were reverberating across Europe. Also, as the domestic economy was suffering from a prolonged recession, Croatia would not be an obvious candidate for the euro introduction, even if someone bothered to spare a serious thought on the euro area expansion. An opportunity to reignite the euro adoption process opened up in 2017, as Croatia exited the Excessive Deficit Procedure, while also making progress in tackling macroeconomic imbalances. Institutional reforms that strengthened the financial architecture of the euro area as well as Bulgarian aspirations to kick-start ERM II talks and ultimately the euro area entry have made it possible to concentrate the minds of EU institutions and euro area member states on setting up a new procedure for a further euro area expansion. In parallel with the international dialogue, an euro adoption strategy was being prepared by the Government and the Croatian National Bank in order to kick-start a public discussion. Quite obviously, Croatia sought to join a different euro area from the one that had existed before the Global financial crisis. Also, the awareness of risks arising from a premature euro introduction was high as scars of the sovereign debt crisis were still fresh. A new process needed to be set up to reflect that the times they are a-changing, to quote the lyrics of Dylans famous anthem. To address these new realities, the ERM II participation was made conditional on a number of measurable reform points as well as on entering into the close cooperation arrangements with the Single Supervisory Mechanism and Single Resolution Mechanism. In mid-2019 Croatia set up an ambitious plan to fulfil all the agreed reform requirements within one year, a time period also needed to perform the asset quality review and stress testing of the banking system required to open up a way into the banking union. The actual moment of deciding on the Croatian ERM II entry coincided with the breakout of the pandemic. While the pandemic shock shrouded with uncertainty the economic outlook, formal requirements for the ERM II entry were met in full by mid-2020, including the positive assessment of the banking system soundness required for participation in the banking union. Thus Croatia entered the ERM II on 13 July 2020, with the central parity set at the level of the current market exchange rate, which was assessed to be in line with long-term averages as well as macroeconomic fundamentals. The exchange rate withstood the fallout in financial markets following the breakout of the pandemic, while initial assessments confirmed that the favourable pre-pandemic external position, expected to deteriorate only moderately, should support it throughout the crisis. The traditional discussion of the ERM II participation in the pre-global financial crisis era used to revolve around the training-room/waiting room metaphor. The dilemma whether participation provides an opportunity for prospective members to strengthen their fundamentals or simply sets a time-frame for them to demonstrate ability to function orderly with an exchange rate anchor marked the early period of the euro. For Croatia, the experience probably more closely resembled that of an airport lounge, a cosy place where you can concentrate on your urgent tasks. The formal exchange rate arrangement, coupled with a swap line from the ECB slightly ahead of the formal ERM II entry, strengthened the credibility of the exchange rate anchor. In such an environment, even the pandemic crisis was not able to derail the process. For a country participating in the ERM II, the euro introduction process is driven by an auto-pilot as the Maastricht criteria remain the only hurdle to the euro introduction. Given favourable macroeconomic developments prior to the Croatian ERM II entry as well as the suspension of the Stability and Growth Pact throughout the pandemic, a quick euro introduction seemed within reach. However, inflation resurgence on the back of the lingering pandemic and the Russian aggression on Ukraine made sure that some uncertainty remained until the very last moment. The inflationary shock has been asymmetric across regions and countries, with Central and Eastern Europe hit particularly hard. Nevertheless, inflation in Croatia moved in line with the EU averages until very recently and even now the inflation rate is the second lowest amongst the Central and Eastern European countries, trailing only behind that of Slovenia, allowing to meet the inflation criterion. Regardless of the subjective dimension, Croatia cannot escape the wider ramification of the euro introduction. For better or worse, it has a potential to serve as a watershed moment towards a more complete monetary union and the engine of further integration. For our part, we intend to do our best to write the history in such a way as to be kind towards our accession, to paraphrase Churchills quote. CROATIAN NATIONAL BANK

Title: EU and Central and Eastern Europe: Productivity and Convergence
text: EU and Central and Eastern Europe: Productivity and convergence* Prof. dr. Boris Vuj?i? Governor of the Since the early 1990s, Central and Eastern European (CEE) countries have undergone a significant institutional and economic transition and most of them are now full members of the European Union (EU). Nevertheless, their economic convergence is not nearly as complete, and the income and productivity gap between CEE and the "old" Europe still exists. Moreover, since the beginning of the global financial crisis in 2008, convergence progress seems to have slowed. In the face of post-crisis challenges, CEE countries will need to find new and more flexible drivers of the convergence process and the establishment of more efficient economic systems for years to come. Let's look at what has been achieved so far and look at where the opportunities for further progress of the economies of CEE countries lie. The meaning of productivity for the relative position of the country The results of the central and eastern European countries, a member of the European Union (EU), since the early 1990s have been remarkable, making them the main driver of growth in Europe and the only example of convergence on the Old Continent. CEE countries initially achieved low levels of productivity compared to "old" Europe. This continued even during the first ten years of transition. The level of productivity was only half of the average of the "old" Europe in 2002. (Figure 1). However, the convergence process was very fast, as evidenced by the growth in productivity. Since the early 2000s, productivity growth in CEE has averaged three times higher than that of the rest of the EU (Figure 2). At the same time, such outputs can be largely attributed to the weak performance of the "old" Europe, which has seen only slight increases in productivity. This process of convergence and attainment of the "old" Europe slowed down slightly during the crisis, but remains present. *Prepared as a basis for the presentation at the conference entitled "Boosting EU Competitiveness 96 The Role of the CESEE Countries", organised by the National Bank of Poland and the Austrian National Bank on 15-16 October 2015. What does the EU's position compare to the US The taking of the "old" EU as a benchmark for CEE countries is driven by its role as the main economic and trading partner of CEE economies, as well as with the aim of creating a common currency area. Also, rapidly changing industries, such as ICT, are vulnerable to shocks and as such should have flexible conditions for employment and redundancy. For this reason, multinationals will endeavour to refrain from starting their businesses in countries with over-regulated labour markets. In the 90s, all large enterprises and all fast-growing enterprises originated in the USA, not in Europe. In addition, evidence shows that the probability of expansion or contraction is higher for US companies, while in Europe it is dominated by old static enterprises (Bravo-Biosca, 2011). It can be said that the forestry concept of creative destruction works much better in the USA than in Europe. The less dynamic growth distribution of companies in Europe points to less experimentation and slower redistribution of resources than less productive to more productive companies, which are two very important drivers of productivity growth. In addition, a higher proportion of static European companies point to a lower level of competitive pressures, potentially damaging productivity growth over the long term. As a result, the process of redistributing the workforce between businesses is slower, making it difficult to grow productivity in Europe. Unfortunately, Europe is failing to create an environment for fast-growing businesses, and this is something that should be a goal for the whole of Europe, not just for CEE countries. Finally, in terms of financial conditions, we can see major differences between the EU and the US in the availability of equity and venture capital financing. Young and prospective businesses need access to sources of funding to support their growth potential. While this issue has been recognised in Europe, there has been little progress, except in rare cases, such as the one in the UK. Figure 8. Source: Global Competitiveness Report 2014/2015, World Economic Forum Long-term perspective One thing that has marked the economic global scene since the early 2000s has been very rapid productivity growth in emerging and developing economies. Not only was Central and Eastern Europe catching up with the "old" Europe, but emerging markets were catching up with developed economies, greatly increasing competitive pressures. Productivity growth in emerging and developing economies peaked around 2007. Since then, productivity growth has slowed in developed and emerging economies. This slowdown for emerging markets appears to be the result of the end of a period of rapid catch-up with developed countries (The Conference Board, 2014, 2015). In addition, globalisation and increased trade integration have reduced barriers to access to different markets and led to the shift of production between countries. The relative price of internationally exchangeable goods decreased, which could have affected long-term developments in inflation rates. More intense global competition is preventing businesses from increasing prices and putting downward pressures on wages in many sectors. This could partly explain the lack of the usual (historical) reaction of inflation rates to the unusual expansionary monetary policies currently implemented by central banks. Globalisation may be the reason for the decrease in the strength of the cyclical response of inflation to fluctuations in domestic production. The prices of numerous products that are produced or consumed at home are increasingly determined by foreign, not local factors of demand and supply. Moreover, financial integration allows for larger shortfalls or surpluses of the trade balance, thus weakening the relationship between domestic production and demand. However, in a globalised, more competitive world, countries which do not have wage flexibility and/or productivity changes, face a relative increase in unit labour costs (ULC), leading to an increase in unemployment rates and/or an increase in public debt in countries that choose to support weak sectors. In the recent financial crisis, the investment-driven economic growth model has been halted. Inflows of foreign capital from the pre-crisis period have dried up sharply, negatively affecting the economic performance in the CEE region (Figure 9). In the post-crisis period, net inflows of foreign direct investment decreased in all countries in the region. In the pre-crisis period, Slovenia was the only exception to net outflows of international investment, while in all other countries there were strong inflows of foreign direct investment (Figure 10). Following the crisis, coupled with a downward investment cycle, the CEE region also faced excessive private sector indebtedness. The accelerated build-up of debt in the run-up to the crisis has raised concerns about the inability to pay down debt during the crisis, triggering a post-crisis deleveraging process. This has put further strain on the investment recovery. Once debt becomes sustainable again and collateral rates increase, only then can we expect investment to restart. Completing the deleveraging process is a necessary but not sufficient condition to re-stimulate the growth of foreign direct investment. It is clear that the CEE region needs to find new drivers of investment, and is more likely to find them in the domestic market, as pre-crisis strong foreign capital inflows are unlikely to happen again any time soon (Dabrowski, 2014). Therefore, today for Central and Eastern Europe, the main challenge is how to change an economic system that was based on imported productivity gains into a system based on endogenous sources of innovation as drivers of growth. But in reality, fiscal policy in the CEE region behaved the opposite of what would be desirable. Fiscal policy is largely pro-cyclical, i.e. pro-cyclical. expansionary before the crisis and restrictive during the crisis (Figure 11). The question arises as to why countries have not adjusted the character of their fiscal policies. The answer is simple 96 because they did not have the fiscal space to do so. If in the good times you were in the wrong place, you will end up in the wrong place and in bad times, which is very similar to the view of macroprudential politics. After years of implementing expansionary policies, states resulted in the accumulation of high deficits and public debt, so that when the crisis hit, countries did not have the fiscal space to implement proactive anticyclical fiscal policies. High debt ratios must now inevitably be reduced and reduced to more sustainable levels. Apart from the Baltic countries, no CEE country, a member of the EU, has yet achieved its medium-term objectives set by the European Commission (Figure 12). In other words, if the fiscal Stability and Growth Pact is to be implemented, public spending should not be a driver of future development, at least not in the medium term. Sources: Eurostat; European Commission In addition to the above challenges, there is also a serious long-term problem, which is the aging of the population. This is a widespread, European, and not only European problem. The population ages faster in Central and Eastern Europe than in "old" Europe, which is why the situation is particularly serious in these countries. The rate of dependent elderly population will double (Figure 13) by 2060. This will not only strain economic growth prospects, but also put additional pressures on the fiscal balance of all countries, albeit at varying intensity. In order to respond to these challenges, the competent authorities will need to rethink the coherence of the labour market and pension and health systems with demographic trends. Measures aimed at increasing the labour force participation rate seem to be an obvious and desirable policy direction, but with reforms of the pension and health systems. Figure 13. Monetary policy may have already done enough, if not too much. Furthermore, there is little or no fiscal space in most countries, especially given the constraints on monetary policy to support cheap state financing in the long run. For too long, a period of extremely low interest rates could become counterproductive as it could encourage austerity more than consumption. Therefore, the CEE region should continue with reforms that increase the productivity of domestic economies, in particular reforms to improve the ease of doing business aimed at reducing the complexity and costs of regulating companies and strengthening legal institutions as well as improving the overall efficiency of the public sector. In conclusion, over the next decade, CEE will have to move away from classic catch-up by imitating and importing productivity gains towards a more flexible system knowledge-based with more added value and more diversified exports. CEE countries will need to further increase capital and labour productivity through their own resources, making investments in education, ICT and research and development essential. Fiscal policies will need to be geared towards restoring sustainability, while macroprudential measures should aim to preserve financial stability and avoid a repeat of episodes of excessive growth. Governments will have to find ways to foster an environment that rewards experimentation, punishes inertia and reduces the cost of failure. This applies not only to CEE countries but also to the whole of Europe, with the aim of building more efficient, dynamic and productive economic systems for years to come. Finally, Europe, and CEE in particular, will need to rethink the alignment of labour markets, pensions and health systems with the slow but safe upcoming challenge of an accelerated population ageing.
