Title: Euro and myths about the euro
text: The euro and the myths of the euro Published: 13.10.2021. Column by Governor Boris Vujcic for the weekly Nacional, published on 12 October 2021. Yuval Noah Harari recently enthroned myths on the pedestal of the highest human achievements. By his firm belief, it was the belief in non-existent things that turned animals, which are not particularly singled out by anything, into humans. But like any human tool, myths , instead of great achievements, can be used for destruction. There are few myths as powerful as standing money - a thing without inherent value that because of trust we are willing to exchange for something that has usable value. The process of replacing the kuna with the euro thus undoubtedly has a mythical dimension, which has fostered the collective imagination and produced a series of recognizable myths, some quite destructive forces. There are currently four truths leading the way that sound plausible, although they are quite inaccurate - about the unwillingness of Croatiafor the euro, about the superiority of an independent monetary policy over participation in the creation of a common monetary policy, about the certainty of a large price increase at the time of the introduction of the euro - and finally, about the unwillingness of the euro area for Croatia (just in case, if with nevertheless, it turns out that Croatia itself is ready for the adoption of the euro). In addition, as counterintuitive as this myth may be - doubts have arisen about the CNB's motives for rushing the euro adoption process, which, in turn, is related to the perception that in the euro area the CNB could stop atwork. Since, according to Orwell's saying, the myths that people believe in tend to become reality, it is important for them to face the real reality in time. "Croatia is not ready for the euro." This myth is not easy to deconstruct -because behind it there is nocoherent economic argument. But the sentence sounds great to those who do not care too much about economic explanations, so they often use it. Unwillingness is usually interpreted as too low a per capita GDP level. According to this myth, the euro would make it more difficult economicallyto catch up with more developed members, i.e. real convergence. However, real convergence is accompanied by nominal convergence, i.e. the gradual convergence of price levels, which are still a third lower in Croatia than the euro area average. Croatia hasbeen very gradually converged over the past decade by both the average level of euro area GDP and the average price level. These processes should continue in the future, meaning that the inflation rate will continue to be slightly higher than the euro area average. If Croatia were to accidentally accelerate real convergence, in or out of the euro area, it would also increase the gap between inflation rates. Maintaining monetary autonomy in such a scenario would force the central bank to allow the nominal flow to gradually strengthenin order to alleviate persistently stronger inflationary pressures. One form of unwillingness is also linked to structural lower interest rates that could stimulate the overheating of the economy, inflation and the cumulation of macroeconomic imbalances and without a real convergen. And it seems that maintaining higher interest rates and allowing exchange rate appreciation, which in this case would be an appropriate monetary policy reaction in the scenario of staying outside the euro area, are exactly the opposite of what Eurosceptics have in mind when they mentionCroatia's alleged unwillingness. "It is important to keep your own currency so that monetary policy can react to the asymmetric shocks affecting the domestic economy." This myth is based on economic theories and insights because monetary policy performsa very useful stabilization function in the wartime and medium term. The myth also gains persuasiveness when the long-term tendency to reduce the euroisation of the financial system is cited as a crowning argument in favour of preserving and strengthening monetary sovereignty, with abreak in kuna funds gradually approaching half of the total sources in banks. However, all the analyses carried out show that the Croatian business cycle is largely in line with the euro area cycle. The coherence of the business cycle is gradually increasing over time, which is not surprising if we have in mind the large and growing economic and financial integration of Croatia with the euro area. Of course, historical developments are not a firm guarantee of the future - one cannot say with certainty that Croatia will never be hit by an asymmetrical showk. The question, however, is whether an independent monetary policy could adequately respond to such distortions. On the other hand, euro area membership gives the CNB the opportunity to "print" the euro to ensure liquidity in crisis situations. Currently, the CNB can generate euro liquidity only to the extent permitted by the engagement of part of the international reserves, which limits monetary policy. Indeed, kuna sources of bank funds are indeed steadily increasing. However, this increase is solely dueto the growth of KUNAS in current and giro accounts - euros have always accounted for over 80 percent of savings and time deposits. Kuna funds in current accounts are always available to citizens and can convene them into euros at any time, which can produce a real "spielcull attack" on the currency. Following the outbreak of the pandemic, the CNB spent 802.7 billion of international reserves in just a few months to alleviate the depreciation pressures that have arisen as businesses and citizens are in a highly crisis situationif it changes kuna assets to euros. And that is why the reduction of euroisation alone does not necessarily mean that the "degrees of freedom" for monetary policy increase, especially in crises, when monetary policy is paramount. Finally, it should not be forgotten that domestic financing provides onlya dj elomic picture. The total debt of all domestic sectors in foreign currency, including foreign debt, stood at as much as EUR 522 billion in the middle of this year. kuna or 141% of GDP. Unfortunately, Euroisation has passed the "point of no return" in Croatia. No country from The Second Year ofWorld War onwards, where the "original sin" of prolonged inflation and hyperinflation reached a scale as in Croatia in the early 1990s, has been able to fully restore all the functions of money to the domestic currency. "Prices will go up a lot, which will violate the living standards of citizens." This myth is less mentioned by trained economists because they are aware that rising prices are not a serious risk. Nevertheless, among the part of the "Eurosceptics" it is extremely popular for a very simple reason - it causes the most fear among citizens. While other bribes aremore abstract in nature, rising prices concern everyone, and many citizens are indeed afraid of price hikes. This fear is greatly the consequence of the widespread perception of price hikes in individual countries following the introduction of the euro. However, official statistics have not confirmedthis perception anywhere. Numerous papers have been written on the divergence of perceived and actual inflation, but we still cannot fully explain this phenomenon. We know for a fact that the introduction of the euro has not caused more price hikes anywhere. Experience has also shown that in termsof accumulation, and at the same time deviations of perception from reality, they are all the smaller the more efficient the mechanisms of control over conversion. A long period of dual price statements and monitoring of how traders will recalculate prices will allow for the immediate identificationof doubtful practices. Of course, we are in a market economy and any trader can change prices at any time. This, after all, is seen in the gradual increase in prices, which in aggregate tends to fluctuate close to the values targeted by central banks. However, there are no reasons why the introduction of the euro itself affects the behaviour of traders, except possibly to a very limited extent when rounding up the prices of fewer goods and services. "The euro area is not ready for Croatia." This myth refers to the unfinished institutional infrastructure of the euro area and the alleged lack of mechanisms to prevent Croatia from turning into a "new Greece". The euro area is really not a full federally-like fiscal union (and it certainly would never become one if eurosceptics were asked). However, the institutional capacity of the euro area has become a glass that has filled up to three quarters in the last decade. The management of fiscal statistics has been transferred from the ministries of finance to independent national bureaus of statistics. Therefore, thereare no longer many potential unpleasant surprises in Croatian j that could affect public debt - it covers debts related to road and railway infrastructure, port authorities and airports, development bank and public television and many other financialobligations of the widely understood public sector. Mechanisms have also been introduced to monitor and correct macroeconomic imbalances, as well as a banking union that is functional in two and a half of the envisaged three pillars (work is still under way to complete the common deposit insurance scheme). Finally, the next generation EU deal also contributes to strengthening the institutional and fiscal capacity of the euro area to prevent crises and manage any future crises. The introduction of the euro will turn the CNB into an outpost of the EUslave central bank." The truth is exactly the opposite of this misconception - after entering the euro area, the CNB will start to use ownership rights over a stake in the European Central Bank in full terms. CNB experts will participate in the work of approximately 160 LA working tiescurrently shaping eurosystem policies in all relevant areas, including the equal participation of the Governors on the ECB's Management Board, which takes decisions on euro area monetary policy. This means that Croatia will change its current monetary sovereignty, which can effectively consume in very small quantities, for the impact on the conduct of the common monetary policy. Information and arguments for discussions on euro area monetary policy will be provided by CNB analysts, and the agreed policy in HVATwill be implemented by the CNB, be it standard or structural repo operations, securities redemption or some third monetary policy instrument. The vast majority of international reserves remain the CNB's assets, which will continue to be managed independently in accordance with common guidelines. Domestic supervisors already make up the majority of the joint supervisory teams under the SSM, while the supervision of smaller banks remains mainly in the CNB's jurisdiction. The CNB will continueto implement macroprudential policy with a greater degree of autonomy, and will also participate in the formulation of resolution policies and the implementation of resolution procedures. In addition, the CNB will manage the local component of the euro area payment system "TARGET-H" and will also acquire the distribuirati cash of the euro. Finally, it should be aware that these myths relate exclusively to the economic dimensions of the decision on the time of adoption of the euro. The decision on the euro is primarily political, although there should certainly be a solid economic analysis behind it. On thestraight, the euro certainly does not guarantee the resolution of all our development problems. And as Seneca Jr. concluded a long time ago, to those who do not know which port they are sailing into, no wind is good. If we set the right economic course, the euro can very well be up to us atleast a tailwind.
text_original: HRVATSKA NARODNA BANKA Euro i mitovi o euru Objavljeno: 13.10.2021. Kolumna guvernera Borisa Vujia za tjednik Nacional, objavljena 12. listopada 2021. Yuval Noah Harari nedavno je mitove ustoliio na pijedestal najviih ljudskih dostignua. Po njegovom vrstom uvjerenju, upravo je vjerovanje u nepostojee stvari pretvorilo ivotinje, koje se niim posebno ne izdvajaju, u ljude. No kao i svaki ljudski alat, i mitovi se, umjesto za velika postignua, mogu koristiti za destrukciju. Malo je mitova monih kao stoje novac - stvar bez inherentne vrijednosti koju smo zbog povjerenja spremni razmjenjivati za neto to ima upotrebnu vrijednost. Proces zamjene kune eurom tako nesumnjivo ima i mitsku dimenziju, koja je potakla kolektivnu imaginaciju i proizvela niz prepoznatljivih mitova, nekih i prilino destruktivne snage. Trenutno prednjae etiri istine koje zvue plauzibilno premda su sasvim netone - o nespremnosti Hrvatske za euro, o superiornosti samostalne monetarne politike nad sudjelovanjem u kreiranju zajednike monetarne politike, o izvjesnosti velikog porasta cijena u trenutku uvoenja eura - i konano, o nespremnosti europodruja za Hrvatsku (za svaki sluaj, ako se ipak ispostavi da je sama Hrvatska spremna za uvoenje eura). Usto, koliko god ovaj mit bio kontraintuitivan - pojavila se i sumnja u motive HNB-a za pourivanje procesa uvoenja eura, koja je, pak, povezana s percepcijom da bi u europodruju HNB mogao ostati bez posla. Kako po Orwellovoj izreci mitovi u koje ljudi povjeruju imaju tendenciju postati stvarnost, vano ihje na vrijeme suoiti s pravom stvarnou. "Hrvatska nije spremna za euro." Ovaj mit nije jednostavno dekonstruirati -jer iza njega ne stoji koherentna ekonomska argumentacija. Ali reenica zvui izvrsno onima koji ne mare previe za ekonomska objanjenja pa je esto koriste. Nespremnost se obino tumai kao preniska razina BDP-a po glavi stanovnika. Euro bi, prema tom mitu, oteao gospodarsko sustizanje razvijenijih lanica, odnosno realnu konvergenciju. No realnu konvergenciju prati i nominalna konvergencija, odnosno postupno pribliavanje razine cijena, koje su u Hrvatskoj jo uvijek treinu nie od prosjeka europodruja. Hrvatska je proteklih desetljea vrlo postupno konvergirala i prema prosjenoj razini BDP-a europodruja i prema prosjenoj razini cijena. Ti bi se procesi trebali nastaviti i ubudue, to znai da e stopa inflacije i dalje biti neto via od prosjeka europodruja. Kada bi Hrvatska sluajno ubrzala realnu konvergenciju, u europodruju ili izvan njega, to bi povealo i razliku meu stopama inflacije. Zadravanje monetarne samostalnosti u takvom bi scenariju prisililo sredinju banku da dopusti postupno jaanje nominalnog teaja kako bi ublaila kontinuirano snanije inflatorne pritiske. Jedan vid nespremnosti vee se i uz strukturne nie kamatne stope koje bi mogle potaknuti pregrijavanje gospodarstva, inflaciju i kumuliranje makroekonomskih neravnotea i bez realne konvergencije. A ini se da su odravanje viih kamatnih stopa i doputanje aprecijacije teaja, koji bi u tom sluaju bili odgovarajua reakcija monetarne politike u scenariju ostanka izvan europodruja, upravo suprotni onome to euroskeptici imaju na umu kad spominju navodnu nespremnost Hrvatske. "Vano je zadrati vlastitu valutu kako bi monetarna politika mogla reagirati na asimetrine okove koji pogaaju domae gospodarstvo." Ovaj je mit utemeljen na ekonomskim teorijama i spoznajama jer monetarna politika u kratkom i srednjem roku obavlja vrlo korisnu stabilizacijsku funkciju. Mit dobiva na uvjerljivosti i kada se kao krunski argument u prilog ouvanju i jaanju monetarne suverenosti navede dugorona tendencija smanjenja euroizacije financijskog sustava s udjelom kunskih sredstava koji se u bankama postupno primie polovici ukupnih izvora. No sve provedene analize pokazuju da je hrvatski poslovni ciklus u velikoj mjeri usklaen s ciklusom europodruja. Usklaenost poslovnog ciklusa postupno raste kroz vrijeme, to ne iznenauje imamo li u vidu veliku i rastuu gospodarsku i financijsku integraciju Hrvatske s europodrujem. Naravno, povijesna kretanja nisu vrsto jamstvo budunosti - ne moe se sa sigurnou tvrditi da Hrvatsku nikada nee pogoditi asimetrian ok. Pitanje je, meutim, bi li i samostalna monetarna politika mogla adekvatno odgovoriti na takve poremeaje. S druge strane, lanstvom u europodruju HNB dobiva mogunost "tiskanja" eura kako bi osigurao likvidnost u kriznim situacijama. Trenutno HNB moe stvarati eursku likvidnost samo u onoj mjeri koliko to doputa angaman dijela meunarodnih priuva, to ograniava monetarnu politiku. Kunski izvori sredstava banaka doista se kontinuirano poveavaju. Meutim, taj je porast iskljuivo rezultat rasta kunskih sredstava na tekuim i iro raunima - euri oduvijek ine preko 80 posto tednih i oroenih depozita. Kunska sredstva na tekuim raunima uvijek su raspoloiva graanima i mogu ih u bilo kojem trenutku konvenirati u eure, to moe proizvesti pravi "pekulativni napad" na valutu. Nakon izbijanja pandemije HNB je u svega nekoliko mjeseci potroio 2,7 milijardi eura meunarodnih priuva kako bi ublaio deprecijacijske pritiske koji su se pojavili jer su poduzea i graani u visoko kriznoj situaciji mijenjali kunsku imovinu u eure. I zato samo smanjenje euroizacije ne znai nuno da se poveavaju "stupnjevi slobode" za monetarnu politiku, osobito u krizama, kad je monetarna politika najvanija. Konano, ne treba zaboraviti da domae financiranje prua tek djelominu sliku. Ukupan dug svih domaih sektora u stranoj valuti, to ukljuuje i inozemni dug, sredinom ove godine iznosio je ak 522 mlrd. kuna ili 141 posto BDP-a. Naalost, euroizacija je u Hrvatskoj prola "toku bez povratka". Nijedna zemlja od Drugog svjetskog rata naovamo u kojoj je "istoni grijeh" dugotrajne inflacije i hiperinflacije dosegnuo razmjere kao u Hrvatskoj poetkom 1990-ih, nije uspjela domaoj valuti potpuno vratiti sve funkcije novca. "Cijene e jako porasti, to e naruiti ivotni standard graana." Ovaj mit manje spominju trenirani ekonomisti jer su svjesni da porast cijena nije ozbiljan rizik. Ipak, meu dijelom "euroskeptika" iznimno je popularan iz vrlo jednostavnog razloga - izaziva najvie straha kod graana. Dok su drugi mitovi apstraktnije naravi, rast cijena se tie svakoga, a mnogi se graani doista i plae poskupljenja. Taj je strah uvelike posljedica rairene percepcije poskupljenja u pojedinim dravama nakon uvoenja eura. Meutim, slubene statistike nigdje nisu potvrdile tu percepciju. Napisani su brojni radovi o razilaenju percipirane i stvarne inflacije, ali taj fenomen i dalje ne moemo do kraja objasniti. Pouzdano znamo da uvoenje eura nigdje nije uzrokovalo vea poskupljenja. Iskustva su takoer pokazala da su poskupljenja, a ujedno i odstupanja percepcije od stvarnosti, tim manja to su mehanizmi nadzora nad konverzijom uinkovitiji. Dugo razdoblje dvojnog iskazivanja cijena i praenje naina na koji e trgovci preraunavati cijene omoguit e trenutno utvrivanje dvojbenih praksi. Naravno, u trinom smo gospodarstvu i svaki trgovac u bilo kojem trenutku moe promijeniti cijene. To se, uostalom, i vidi u postupnom rastu cijena koji u agregatu uglavnom oscilira blizu vrijednosti koje ciljaju sredinje banke. No nema nikakvih razloga da samo uvoenje eura utjee na ponaanje trgovaca, osim eventualno u vrlo ogranienoj mjeri kod zaokruivanja cijena manjeg broja dobara i usluga. "Europodruje nije spremno za Hrvatsku." Taj se mit odnosi na nedovrenu institucionalnu infrastrukturu europodruja i navodni manjak mehanizama kojima bi se sprijeilo pretvaranje Hrvatske u "novu Grku". Europodruje doista nije potpuna fiskalna unija nalik federalnoj zajednici (i to sigurno ne bi nikad ni postala ako se pita euroskeptike). Meutim, institucionalni kapacitet europodruja je u posljednjem desetljeu postao aa koja se napunila do tri etvrtine. Voenje fiskalnih statistika prebaeno je iz ministarstava financija u neovisne nacionalne zavode za statistiku. Stoga ni u Hrvatskoj vie ne postoji mnogo potencijalnih neugodnih iznenaenja koja bi mogla utjecati na javni dug - on obuhvaa dugove vezane uz cestovnu i eljezniku infrastrukturu, luke kapetanije i zrane luke, razvojnu banku i javnu televiziju i jo mnogo drugih financijskih obaveza iroko shvaenog javnog sektora. Uvedeni su i mehanizmi za nadzor i ispravljanje makroekonomskih neravnotea, kao i bankovna unija koja je funkcionalna u dva i pol od predviena tri stupa (jo uvijek se radi na dovretku zajednikog sustava osiguranja depozita). Konano, dogovor o EU-u sljedee generacije takoer pridonosi jaanju institucionalnih i fiskalnih kapaciteta europodruja za sprjeavanje kriza i upravljanje eventualnim buduim krizama. Uvoenje eura pretvorit e HNB u ispostavu Europske sredinje banke." Istina je upravo suprotna od ove zablude - HNB e nakon ulaska u europodruje poeti u punom smislu koristiti vlasnika prava nad udjelom u Europskoj sredinjoj banci. Strunjaci HNB-a sudjelovat e u radu otprilike 160 radnih tijela koja trenutno oblikuju politike eurosustava u svim relevantnim podrujima, ukljuujui i ravnopravno sudjelovanje guvernera u Upravnom odboru ESB-a koji donosi odluke o monetarnoj politici europodruja. To znai da e Hrvatska trenutni monetarni suverenitet, koji faktino moe konzumirati u vrlo malim koliinama, mijenjati za utjecaj na voenje zajednike monetarne politike. Informacije i argumentacije za rasprave o monetarnoj politici europodruja pruat e HNB-ovi analitiari, a usuglaenu politiku u Hrvatskoj e provoditi HNB, bilo da je rije o standardnim ili strukturnim repo operacijama, otkupu vrijednosnih papira ili nekom treem instrumentu monetarne politike. Ogromna veina meunarodnih priuva ostaje imovina HNB-a kojom e on i dalje samostalno upravljati u skladu sa zajednikim smjernicama. Domai supervizori ve sada ine veinu zajednikih supervizorskih timova u okviru Jedinstvenog nadzornog mehanizma, dok nadzor manjih banaka i dalje ostaje uglavnom u ingerenciji HNB-a. HNB e i nadalje s velikom dozom autonomije provoditi makrobonitetnu politiku, a sudjelovat e i u oblikovanju sanacijskih politika i provedbi postupaka sanacije. Usto e HNB upravljati lokalnom komponentom platnog sustava europodruja "TARGET-H" te e pribavljati i distribuirati gotovinu eura. Na kraju, valja biti svjestan toga da se navedeni mitovi odnose iskljuivo na ekonomske dimenzije odluke o trenutku uvoenja eura. Odluka o euru prije svega je politika, iako iza nje svakako treba stajati i solidna ekonomska analiza. Naravno, euro sasvim sigurno ne jami rjeavanje svih naih razvojnih problema. A kao to je Seneka Mlai davno zakljuio, onima koji ne znaju u koju luku plove, nijedan vjetar nije dobar. Postavimo li ispravan gospodarski kurs, euro nam itekako moe biti dobar vjetar u lea. text: Dr. 8eeljko Rohatinski And U R O Thesis for presentation at the forum of the Association "Advanced Croatia HR" on open issues of euro adoption in the Republic of Croatia, Zagreb, 19 June 2007. General settings: InLasko, the European Union (EU) also assumes the obligation to join the European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). Timing can be flexible, but there is no full integration without entering the monetary union, which in turn is treated as a "reward" for responsible and successful policies while in the "purgatory" of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM). It is widely believed that the introduction of the euro alone will solve many problems or will at least make it much easier to solve them. The rational part of this belief is based on theoretical settings and past experience on the benefits of membership of the monetary union, namely, among others: - increasing exchanges - eliminating exchange rate risk, reducing real interest rates and increasing attractiveness for foreign direct investment (FDI) - reduction in transaction costs (0.4% of GDP) - strengthening discipline in macroeconomic policy making. Costs Initial models of optimal currency areas - 2 criteria: 1. susceptibility to asymmetric shocks of supply and demand, 2. efficiency of non-monetary instruments of adjustment to shocks. Susceptibility to shocks is less the more similar the structure of production and the greater its diversification. The efficiency of non-monetary instruments depends on the flexibility of prices and wages and the mobility of the workforce (protection of employees, the level of concluding of collective agreements, the level of the minimum wage, etc.), as well as on the possibility of countercyclical action of fiscal policy (automatic fiscal stabilizer) i.e. on the sensitivity of the budget to economic fluctuations and the amount of the fiscal multiplier. The basic assumption is the success of the exchange rate as a mechanism for eliminating asymmetric shocks because (according to the theory) its change allows for the rapid adjustment of relative prices. However, empirical research shows that the variability of the real exchange rate is greater than the variability of the nominal exchange rate, and this means that changes in the nominal exchange rate in practice do not follow the price differential. Furthermore, the exchange rate is not a good mechanism for eliminating asymmetric shocks of monetary and financial character that do not require changes in relative prices. Bottom line: the exchange rate functions more as a source than as a shock dampener, so the cost of losing exchange rate sovereignty is not great either. (This should be remembered.) The essence of the problem lies in the differences of economic power of individual actors in the single monetary and financial market where the stronger, in accordance with their interests, profile the basic relationships and tendencies in that market, which in turn can lead to asymmetric shocks of supply and demand. The choice of timing is related to the perception of the initial state of the individual economy and the assessment within which time it is possible to meet the criteria and function efficiently in the monetary union in relation to the opportunities offered by autonomous monetary policy (if possible to lead it). Three approaches: 1. Quick entry (Lithuania, Estonia and Slovenia; members of the ERM since mid-2004)) 2. Slower entry (Cyprus, Latvia and Malta; MEMBERS of the ERM since mid-2005, while Hungary and Slovakia are not members of the ERM and are expected to become members around 2010) 3. Pristup "Wait and see" (Czechia and Poland; larger countries that can conduct monetary policy autonomously) Regardless of the approach, the essence and form remain the same: Formal requirement: nominal convergence (Maastricht criteria in the period in the ERM) The essence of the problem: real convergence (high rate of long-term sustainable growth, linked to the Copenhagen criterion of the ability to cope with the pressure of competition and market relations within the EU). In doing so, nominal convergence previously established is considered to be a precondition for real convergence. Current situation: High degree of substantive (non-institutional and passive) integration into the EU in the conditions of the already implemented liberalisation of the financial system: -practically 2/3 of the exchange; the full dominance of foreign banks, investment and pension funds and leasing companies owned by the EU; foreign ownership of strategic sectors and euroisation of the financial system (65% of savings) as a reflection of the structure of the source of savings and limited confidence in the national currency. The inflow of capital on these grounds (primarily through credit relations) substantially determines the exchange rate of the kuna and the overall monetary policy. Operational objective of monetary policy: Stability of the nominal exchange rate (prevention of appreciation) at the level of liquidity combined with such a exchange rate will be sufficient to finance sustainable growth at low inflation. Basic instrumentation: Devious interventions with administrative restrictions on the inflow of financial capital and its monetary multiplication: - foreign exchange ( 32%) - marginal reserve requirement (55%) - credit control (16%, 12 %) - reserve requirement (17%) - prudential measures (differentiated capital adequacy, currency-induced risk) open market operations (fine-tuning to stabilise interest rates - no bid) Restrictions: direct lending from abroad, foreign currency loans. Results (together with the Ministry of Finance and the Government of the Republic of Croatia): Andwe meet the Maastricht criteria with an average growth of 4.7% per year (between 2001 and 2006), at the growth of loans of 20% and the money mass of 18%. Fences: pensioner debt, long-term bonds, harmonised consumer price index However: In practice, we have the classic Tinbergen problem of "conflict of objectives" due to the disproportion between the number of instruments and objectives (more objectives than instruments). In addition, due to the low efficiency of the overall economy and the efficiency of allocation and use of money, monetary policy cannot be restrictive in the literal sense. At the same time, high yield rates make banks' interest rates still poorly elastic to the costs imposed by the CNB, and it is realistic to assume the low elasticity of demand. Problems: 1. Payment deficit 7-8% (supports low inflation) and foreign debt 85% of GDP 2. "Bubbl" in the real estate and securities market (property prices between 2002 and 2006 averaged 8.7%; stock index in 2004-2006 averaged 40%) 3. Real appreciation of the exchange rate in 2006 compared to 2001: 11% deflated by consumer prices 14% deflated by unit (gross) labour costs Related to 1, this indicates an imbalanced exchange rate (although the payment deficit also arises from structural reasons, hypertrophied by lending from abroad), while the comparison of unit costs shows that the exchange rate does not offset the disparity of these costs. 4. Immobilised liquidity: (HRK 83bn or 30% of banks' total liabilities, corresponding to 45% of total liquid assets) due to measures aimed at preventing appreciation 5. Vulnerability to exchange rate and interest rate changes, which will exist until entering emu. For example, the 10% depreciation of the kuna increases the gross debt of the non-financial sector to banks and abroad by EUR 33 billion. kuna or by 12% of GDP, while net debt (minus savings) would increase by 7% of GDP (whereby the structure of the debtor is by no means coincident with the structure of the savers). All this, with a payment effect (expressed in nominal kunas, assuming 50% elasticity of exports) does not exceed 2% of GDP, and with the raising of inflation to the level of about 6% with a negative impact on real incomes and domestic demand. With such overall performance, one can hardly expect a dynamic of sustainable growth that leads to real convergence relatively quickly. According to the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) estimates, with growth dynamics of 4.7% and continued depopulation (0.47%) to reach the average GDP per capita of Greece, Portugal and Spain, Croatia takes 29 years (Slovenia 3, Czech Republic 17, Poland 39, Bulgaria 25, Romania 23). Joining the EU lifts the main restrictions and thus the way monetary policy is implemented so far. In this sense, the question arises, among others, how to treat the exchange rate. Initial position: We want to introduce the euro as soon as possible (2 years). We enter the ERM immediately, with the European Central Bank (ECB) we set the middle exchange rate and then the conversion exchange rate, which we publish, thus making it the anchor of exchange rate expectations until entering the EMU. Basic dilemma: How to determine the middle course when entering the ERM, i.e. what it is exchange rate level: the level of the market exchange rate found or the target level of the exchange rate closer to cost parity? Determination of the middle exchange rate: It is a function of two elements: exchange rate expectations and fundamental determinants. After 5 years of hard "ironing", expectations of significant changes in the exchange rate are small. It remains a matter of funds. Arguments"for"targeted baselines of financial resources: The real appreciation of the exchange rate so far and the reduction of pressures on the real adjustment of costs in order to increase competitiveness on the just entering the single market The arguments "against" such a course: - activating all exchange rate risks - financial impact on debtors - budgetary problems - impulse to increase inflation initially - reducing domestic demand with a possible negative impact on production - social problems - small payment base effects Initial assumptions for achieving a target exchange rate if the "yes" arguments prevailed: 1. Prevent further appreciation pressures (If necessary, further tighten and extend restrictions on foreign capital inflows and substitute some of this inflow by releasing banks' immobilised liquidity for the sustainable growth of domestic loans. This is only possible before entering the EU, even if we do not immediately enter the ERM, because only until then can we use monetary restrictions.) We tried this in 2006 - to no avail. There is a risk of reducing international reserves, in conditions where foreign gross financing needs (in the period 2007-2010), assuming a gradual reduction of the current account deficit of the balance of payments and a stagnation of the debt-to-GDP ratio, average about 32% (net 11%, of which foreign direct and portfolio investments are about 5% and net loans are about 6% of GDP). 2. Prevent depreciation to variable costs (salaries, taxes) to spill over This requires the determination of the Government of the Republic of Croatia and a broader consensus. A psychological problem would also arise: joining the EU means a real pay cut. 3. Withprevent the re-formation of depreciation and inflation expectations, i.e. the "escape" of savings from kuna to foreign currency 1st and partially 2. prefers a gradualist approach, and 3. shock therapy, without prior notice. The price of this would be the loss of some of the CNB's hard-won credibility, with the very problematic assumption that the ECB would accept such a exchange rate. That is why, when determining the middle exchange rate of the kuna, the Government of the Republic of Croatia plays a key role because it will depend on the overall economic policy and have feedback implications for it. However, whatever the middle exchange rate, it in itself will not significantly change the tendencies in the movement of fundamental financial determinants of its current formation, so in unchanged conditions the "target" exchange rate can provide only a short-term "respite" in effecting the pressures of these determinants on its further real appreciation. With this in mind and summing up all the potentially positive effects of exchange rate depreciation, economic and political preconditions for nominal depreciation to be both a real depreciation and the economic and social costs of such an operation, an attempt to initially depreciate the exchange rate to a hypothetical equilibrium level would not be rational. ERM: After entering the ERM, the market exchange rate can fluctuate up to 15 percent from the middle one (without the possibility of devaluation, without capital controls, but also with the right of the ECB to suspend interventions towards appreciation if they are not necessary for price stability). However, as other Maastricht criteria should be maintained at the same time, large fluctuations in the market exchange rate are very risky, and will continue to need a hard "ironing" (foreign exchange interventions, open market operations, perhaps currency board) with enhanced prudential measures as a substitute for the monetary restrictions so far, and with the establishment of a mechanism for the gradual release of immobilised liquidity. In this sense, the adoption of the Law on Credit Institutions (ZOKI) is also significant, but there is a risk that a strong tightening of prudential measures will lead to daughter banks starting to turn into branches of foreign banks. In addition, as prudential measures can be expected to be less effective than monetary restrictions, already in the PERIOD of the ERM it will be necessary to meet the corrections of the corrections of the corresponding political and tax payments. Without this, in the conditions of the continued inflow of foreign capital, allowing further real appreciation of the exchange rate with an increasing payment-balance deficit would be the only obstacle to increasing inflation. On the other hand, falling prices and wage rigidity can make adjusting the overvalued exchange rate difficult and expensive from the point of view of employment and future growth. So economic policy will have to be very sensitive and balanced. "Recommendations" of international financial institutions for EMU: 1. Low fiscal deficit and reduction of the rigidity of subsidies and automatism of determined social transfers in order to achieve a primary surplus. This could also duly service public debt without having a negative impact on the economy in the face of large fluctuations in demand and fluctuations in production growth. 2. Wage and price flexibility must be protected where it is present and encouraged where it is weak. 3. Strong synchronisation of activities with the eurozone. The stronger it is, the less asymmetrical the cyclical action of a single monetary policy will be. 4. Strong supervision of the financial system. 5. With the ECB, set the median exchange rate on entry into the ERM and the emu entry conversion rate, which will establish an appropriate degree of competitiveness. So, what we know ourselves. Conclusion: By entering the EU, one should not expect spectacular changes in the area of the exchange rate compared to the current situation and the situation as it should be, or should be, without entering the ERM and EMU. The greatest benefit will be the cessation of barren discussions about the course as a "magic wand" to solve all problems. This will force us to take a more serious approach to the true causes of these problems and their elimination.

Title: Presentation at the Annual Economic Conference of the Faculty of Economics in Zagreb
text: Presentation by Prof. Dr. Boris Vujcic at the Annual Economic Conference of the Faculty of Economics in Zagreb Published: 29.10.2012. Speech Prof. Dr. Boris Vujcic, CNB Governor 29.10.2012. Annual Economic Conference 2012 Zagreb, Faculty of Economics 26.10.2012. Croatia has been in a de facto recession for four years. From 2009 to 2011, GDP decreased by 8.3 percent, and this year we expect it to decrease by a further approximately 1.9 percent, which will increase the cumulative drop in GDP over the last four years to about 10 percentage points. Only next year it is possible to expect the beginning of a slight recovery. Growth,intertime m, is just a summary of many features of the economy. The growth model in Croatia in the ten years before the beginning of the crisis was based primarily on the significant use of foreign capital. Foreign direct investment - 'good cholesterol' - for the most part ended up in the sectorin internationally unstoppable goods and services, while 'bad cholesterol' - the inflow of capital of a debt character - has predominantly ended up in wage growth, loans, i.e. growth in personal consumption, or in infrastructure government investment projects, which are to any extent unable to generate cash flows to service this debt capital. According to the IMF survey, between 2000-2011 the contribution of capital to GDP growth in Croatia was an average of 2.3% per year, technological progress was 0.2% and labour 0%. Therefore, no miracle gives Croatia at the beginning of the crisis, when the inflow of capital ceased, lost its ability to grow. Engagement of work, production and process innovations and technological progress, namely, in Croatia, unfortunately, are not effective growth factors . Today Croatia is at an important, I would say, although I do not like too many words, an almost fateful crossroads. This time he chooses not a political destiny, such as leaving Yugoslavia and becoming independent in 1991, nor joining the EU twenty years later, but his owninto a future economic destiny. The current model of economic development, which was based mainly on the inflow of debt capital, is broken and irreparable. Not only that, but it leaves essential constraints on rapid and successful growth in the future. External debt ofd 100 percent of GDP, public debt fast approaching the limit of 60 percent of GDP, poor economic structure, without sufficiently large number of companies involved in international supply chains, slow and unreliable state-administrative and judicial justiceav, pension insurance system with growing deficits, inefficiently structured health system, education system at the bottom of European rankings of excellence, a large part of agriculture with low productivity and relatively high indebtedness, rigid workcapitalization with low overall employment and partial-time employment, to name just a few of the most significant structural problems. As a result of numerous structural inefficiencies, Croatia has for years had an unacceptable low place in the rankings that evaluate the business climate in individual countries, and the latest World Bank report shows that there is no progress in this regard. These are very serious restrictions on the future development of our country. However, they are not insurmountable, with a decisive promyen of the economic development model. What is worrying is that instead of a new, different economic policy, recently patterns of old failed policies have been offered again. Sometimes out of ignorance, sometimes out of populism, and often as a combination of both. Nknowledge is always bad, sometimes dangerous, and populism is especially dangerous in times of crisis. People, dissatisfied with unsuccessful politicians, jaded by the crisis, falling standards and debt problems, become more inclined to accept seemingly simple and painless solutions to difficult problems, and those who offer them are never lacking. Suggestions that the solution to the problem in Croatia today can be found outside the framework of macroeconomic stability are a very dangerous illusion. Both the policy of devaluation of the exchange rate of the domestic currency and fiscal expansion and monetar financing of the deficit has been tried many times during Yugoslavia, and partly in an independent Croatia. And every time it fell through. Then why are some calling out to her again? Either because they're not able to learn, or because it's the easiest solution to offer. Difficult and unpopular structural reforms should not be implemented - everything is easily solved by printing money, devaluation and borrowing for government spending. Very seductive, especially for those who forget history. If you were right, I have to admit, it would be tabout great. Why would Germans, Danes, Dutch, Austrians and other successful EU countries stick to hard currency, low deficit, wage policy control, and raising productivity through technological innovation and improving production processes for decades after World War II ? When they could simply achieve competitiveness and social prosperity through high domestic and external deficits, money printing and devaluations. Why in these countries is the employment rate between 70 and 75 percent (percentage forthe fallen aged 15-64), versus Croatia's 52.4 percent, which is a lower employment rate than any EU country, including Greece, which with an employment rate of 56 percent is the worst country in the EU? Why, after all, did Yugoslavia not become an export power with so many dinar devaluations? In a situation where the external debt is 102% of GDP, in which the annual total need of foreign (re)financing is 35-36% of GDP, and in which only the state has to finance about an additional approx. A 805 billion deficit this year and the next two years, any loss of macroeconomic stability, fiscal or monetary, in the form of a rapid resumption of public debt growth over 60 percent and/or a devaluation of the domestic currency exchange rate, would lead to a loss of investor confidence and an inability to refinance liabilities on sustainable terms. Public debt has risen from 29.3% of GDP to around 53% since 2008 and is clearly on an unsustainable trajectory, as both rating agencies and the IMF and investors warn. To ignore this warning and invoke, in these conditions, the so-called Keynesian solutions is to not understand the economic and financial risks to the country and to offer people the very dangerous illusion that it can still be as usual. It is similar to the invocation of devaluation in conditions not only high external forprolongation, but also very high domestic savings in foreign currency, that is, the euro. The direct consequence of the devaluation of the domestic currency would be to spoil all the indebtedness indicators relevant to the assessment of the vulnerability of the domestic economy, the credit rating and thus the confidence of the investitora. Also, the devaluation in the conditions of currency substitution, i.e. the high euroization of the passive foreign balance sheet of the state, the enterprise and the majority of indebted households, acts pro-recession, reducing GDP growth through a decrease in investment, personal and state potof employment due to the growth of relative indebtedness. Already in the new edition of the Handbook of monetary economics , a special chapter will be dedicated to the specifics of monetary policy in conditions of high currency substitution, and at the last meeting of the G-30, the most respectableworld gathering of economists, in Tokyo last week, all participants were given precisely a paper explaining why active exchange rate policy is inefficient in the case of small open countries. Especially if they are highly dollarised/euroised. Unfortunately, contemporary literature doesn't seem to be followed by even those for whom it should be a job, easily, it shouldn't even be read. In this country, we can write it, after all the mistakes of the past. One of them, which is reappearing these days, is the nostalgia for state banking. For years, we have heard that Croatia needs state banks, how Croatia has made a mistake by privatising them, that it should look to Slovenia, that state banks exist elsewhere in Europe. But today, after everything that has happened with state banks from the former Yugoslavia, Croatia, Slovenia, Spain or even Austria and Germany, continuing to call for a return to state banking really means that the learning curve for some people is discontinuous. But let's get away from discussions that, in essence,fall out of the past. Where are we today and what can we expect? I would say that there are two imperatives before Croatia. The first is to preserve macroeconomic stability, because without it the crisis will only deepen. What is positive this fall is the fact that the credit rating and investor confidence have been preserved, in difficult conditions. This is due to the sitting side of the start of fiscal consolidation and the announced reduction of the budget deficit and the introduction of fiscal discipline and, on the other hand, the fact that the financial system in Croatia isstable and profitable, primarily due to the corresponding macroprudential policies implemented before the beginning of the crisis. Some countries in Europe have run into serious difficulties and lost market confidence because their fiscal situation has become anon-state due to high budget deficits and high public debt, and refinancing these deficits has become so expensive that they are failing to stop the growth of public debt. It is the so-called snowball effect, when due to high debt the country loses the confidenceof investitors and has to borrow at ever higher interest rates, which requires an increasing fiscal contraction to stop the further growth of public debt due to the increase in interest costs of its servicing. Another part of the countries, such as Iceland, Ireland, Spainof Jol and Slovenia, got into serious trouble primarily because they failed to preserve the stability of the financial system, and due to the losses of the banking system and the realized or potential fiscal costs associated with these losses, they lost theirfinancial markets and faced a downgrade and a large increase in borrowing costs. In order to maintain market confidence, however, Croatia must crediblely continue the process of fiscal consolidation, which will put the public debt-to-GDP ratio ona downward trajectory. In doing so, it should be taken into account that reducing the deficit through reducing expenditure is less detrimental to growth than through an increase in the tax press. Fiscal consolidation this year is happening mainly on the revenue side, rather than the expenditure side of the proll, which, in addition to the larger than expected decline in foreign demand and underperformance of investments, will lead to a larger-than-expected drop in GDP, and the execution of the planned deficit reduction is questionable. If it wants to reduce the negative impact of fiscal consolidationon growth, the government must focus it on the expenditure side, rather than the revenue side of the budget. Another imperative is to find a new growth model. The time for "easy" growth based on the increase in debt capital has passed. Razine external and public indebtedness of 102 percent and 53 percent of GDP, simply no longer allow this growth model. What's that mean? This means that in the short term we cannot expect either public or personal consumption to be the main lever of growth. With domestic, nashlost, the external environment is not stimulating either and cannot significantly stimulate domestic growth: Italy is expected to see a 2.3 percent drop in GDP this year, a decline of -0.7 percent in 2013, with only a slight recovery of 0.5 percent growth in 2014. Another major foreign tradeand partner, Germany, slowed last year's growth of 3.1 percent to an expected 0.9 percent this year and next, and to 1.4 percent in 2014. The most important trading partner in the neighbourhood - Slovenia - is expected to see a 2.2% drop in GDP this year and -0.4% next godina, and a moderate recovery in 2014 of 1.7% of GDP growth. Thus, it is not foreign demand that in itself will be able to generate significant growth, despite joining the EU next year. The only way to make exports an effective factor of economic growth in the short/medium term is, therefore, by increasing the share of Croatian exports on international markets, since aggregate foreign demand on traditional export markets will not increase significantly. This, in turn, will be very difficult to achieve without attracting foreign investment to the export sector, and an increased investment in domestic primary energy sources may also play a certain role in increasing net exports. In general, it seems that too much emphasis is placed on state investment projects, especially bearing in mind theaggravated capacity for government and quasi-state borrowing, and too little on private investments. And it is private investments, especially attracting private capital to export or import substitutive sectors that are what is necessary for the rapid change of the growth model in Croatia. This is what can raise the potential GDP growth rate in the medium term. The experience of small open countries that have successfully developed the export industry shows that foreign investment has played a key role in this. From Ireland, to Estonia, Hungary and the Czech Republic, to Slovakia, the share of foreign-owned enterprises in the total or commodity exports of these countries is at the level of about 80, and even more, percent. In Croatia, this is 47 per cent excluding INA and 53 per cent including INA, at a lower level of exports to GDP. For those who still think that the solution to the problem of Croatian exports lies in the devaluation of the exchange rate of the domestic currency, it should also be said that by the beginning of the crisis, the fastest export growth rate in Central and Eastern Europe was achieved by Slovakia,a country that was also faced with by far the strongest real appreciation of the exchange rate of the domestic currency of over 40 percent, while Croatia, with a much softer appreciation of the real exchange rate, of ten percent, achieved the slowest growth in exports. If the exchange rate were the dominant determinantof exports, it would hardly be possible. The main difference between the two countries - foreign direct investment in the export sector. In other words, Croatia must again base growth on capital inflows, but this time not debt, but direct. It should be said that until nowCroatia has also had an objectively significant drawback in attracting foreign export-oriented investments because it was not a member of the EU. From next year, this shortage disappears and Croatia must seize this opportunity if it wants to return relatively quicklyto the trajectory of growth and job creation. The environment is not in our favour, because this is not in 2004 or 2007, but a time of deep crisis in Europe, but it just means that it is necessary to think boldly and be determined to break down obstacles for business and investashing in Croatia. In this regard, this week's fact that Croatia has fallen from a very bad position by an additional four places in one of the rankings that measure the business/investment climate does not encourage. It should be an alarm and help to redefine the prioof economic policy. If there is a place to make radical moves then it is precisely in this area. In fact, it will not be enough just to solve existing obstacles for business/investment in Croatia, but also to be innovative and enterprising in creating conditions thatare better than in other countries. If it fails to become attractive for business and attract significant investments, Croatia, with high debt levels limits, will find it difficult to establish a functioning growth model. This could condemn the country to a relatively low stope growth in the coming years. This will then define the standard of living of this and future generations. The pension system has long been in deep crisis and the employment rate is the lowest in Europe. These are problems that can affect in the long run a relative declinein the standard of living in Croatia versus other countries. The worst thing would be for the best educated, you young people, faced with poor job opportunities, to decide to look abroad for a better tomorrow. You're that capital, human, that's the most important, and without which there's no developmentand. To go back to the beginning in the end. The choice of the economic future, the redefinition of the growth model and the choice of compliant economic policies is so important for Croatia today, that again the political and general social consensus on the goal and the way of reaching itis desirable. At least among the most relevant social and political forces. If it does not exist, particularinterests and populist impulses threaten to block processes that are in the interest of Croatia, all its citizens in the long run, and most of all of you, and most of all of you, who, I hope, have a whole work career ahead of them (probably up to the age of 70) and, then, a comfortable retirement in the most beautiful country in Europe.
